headline: Ukraine war truce in Kherson area set to expire
description: The rare pause in fighting, which began early Tuesday, enabled a humanitarian mission to Russian-occupied Oleshky.
author: AFP
article_text:
KYIV: The longest truce of the Ukraine war, brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump and limited to just the Kherson region, was set to end on Sunday evening after neither side announced an extension.

The rare pause in fighting, which began early Tuesday, enabled a humanitarian mission to Russian-occupied Oleshky.

Neither side reported violations after the truce began, in what one Ukrainian lawmaker described as the “biggest de-escalation since 2022”.

A Kherson resident said the ceasefire had been a “breath of fresh air”.

“We have to use this time to get things done,” said Volodymyr Omeltc­henko, a 38-year-old gardener. “We’re pruning the rose bushes for winter.”

The ceasefire was due to end later on Sunday.

A Ukrainian military officer expressed concerns that the fighting would be “worse than before” when it resumed as Russian forces, positioned on the other side of the Dnipro river, have taken advantage of the calm of the past few days to amass new troops, transport ammunition stocks.

Refinery hit

Fighting continued elsewhere in Ukraine.

Russia said on Sunday that a drone had struck an “industrial enterprise” east of Moscow overnight.

Ukrainian media reported that Kyiv had attacked the Kstovo oil refinery, calling it “one of Russia’s largest oil refineries, producing fuel and lubricants”.

Kyiv has repeatedly struck Russian oil and gas sites, in what it says is fair retaliation for Russian attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure.

US President Trump had been pressing Kyiv to stop such attacks, blaming them for rising diesel costs that analysts attribute to the Iran war.

Published in Dawn, November 2nd, 2026

headline: SITUATIONER: What is behind the PPP’s push for electoral reforms?
description: Party claims it wants transparent polls, but insiders say it fears PTI will resort to rigging; govt says electoral restructuring was its own initiative.
author: Syed Irfan Raza
article_text:
• Party claims it wants transparent polls, but insiders say it fears PTI ‘will resort to rigging’• Govt says electoral restructuring was its own initiative

THE PPP has stepped up its efforts for electoral reforms in the country, raising several questions: is the party anticipating early general elections, a drastic change in the system, or is it seeking timely reforms to avert potential rigging in the next polls?

On the other hand, the government claims that the initiative was its own rather than the PPP’s, aiming to bring all parties, including the opposition, to the table to reach a consensus on how to prevent rigging in general elections.

It also believes that if the opposition joins the proposed Parliamentary Committee on Electoral Reforms, it will pave the way for dialogue between the government and the opposition on other key issues, including the long-awaited appointment of a new chief election commissioner (CEC).

Background conversations with PPP leaders revealed that the party feared that the main opposition PTI could turn the tables at any time in the next elections with the help of Form-47 “manipulation” (a mechanism of pre-poll rigging of which the PTI itself claims to be a victim).

In the recent past, PPP delegations have met the leader of the opposition in the National Assembly, Mehmood Achakzai, and the leader of the opposition in the Senate, Raja Nasir Abbas, urging them to sit down with the government to discuss the much-needed electoral reforms.

Parliamentary bodies

In a recent speech in the NA, PPP Chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari urged Mr Achakzai to use the “authority and power” delegated to him by jailed PTI founder Imran Khan to direct opposition members to participate in parliamentary committees and discuss pressing national issues.

He said that since parliament had decided, on a motion moved by the PPP, to constitute a committee on electoral reforms, the opposition leader should nominate a representative to the committee and submit their name to the speaker’s office.

Recalling that the opposition had described electoral rigging as its “fundamental issue”, he said, “If we make efforts to bring all stakeholders together in a committee or arrange a briefing on terrorism, economic, and security issues without the opposition’s participation, it will be pointless.”

Speaking to Dawn, PPP General Secretary Nayyar Bukhari said the party was not anticipating early elections; rather, efforts were being made to ensure transparent polls. He said it was the right time to initiate the electoral reform process because the government was about to complete three years of its five-year term. “In the final year of a five-year term, political parties usually launch their election campaigns and don’t concentrate on other issues. Therefore, this is the right time for political parties to sit down together and introduce timely reforms unanimously,” he added.

He was of the view that parliamentary committees were an essential part of legislation and parliamentary democracy. Dismissing the opposition’s demand for equal representation on the proposed committee, he questioned: “When representation in parliament is not equal, how is equality possible in committees?”

He added that electoral reforms would reduce the scope for post-election allegations and disputes, and that including the opposition would further strengthen the legislative process. He said the leader of the opposition in the NA should meet Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif regarding the appointment of the CEC and two members of the Election Commission.

‘Hidden hand’

Meanwhile, a PPP insider said the party feared that the PTI, which is currently in opposition, could turn the tables with the help of a “hidden hand” and win the next general elections through pre-poll rigging.

He added that alongside this concern, the PPP chairman genuinely wanted timely electoral reforms to make the country’s electoral process flawless, fair, and acceptable to all.

When contacted, Ahmed Bilal Mehboob, president of the Pakistan Institute of Legislative Development and Transparency (Pildat), said he did not foresee early elections in the country.

He agreed that it was the right time to launch the electoral reform process because political parties still had sufficient time to rectify the electoral system before the next general election.

Mr Mehboob, however, noted that there was a possibility of a system reset, which might have broader implications.

He said it was a good initiative to take the opposition on board regarding electoral reforms, adding that the government and the opposition should also sit down together to appoint a new chief election commissioner, as the incumbent CEC, Sikandar Sultan Raja, remains in office despite his term expiring two years ago.

Under the 26th Constitutional Amendment, the incumbent CEC can continue to serve after the expiry of his term until a successor is appointed. The Constitution requires the prime minister to consult the leader of the opposition in the NA on the names proposed for the new CEC.

“I cannot understand why the leader of the opposition is not accepting the prime minister’s invitation to sit together for consultation on the new chief election commissioner,” he added.

Federal Minister for Parliamentary Affairs Tariq Fazal Chaudhry told Dawn that the initiative to form the parliamentary committee was taken by NA Speaker Sardar Ayaz Sadiq, not the PPP.

He added that he would begin meeting parliamentary leaders of all parties from today (Monday) to invite them to join the committee on electoral reforms. The minister said there was no reason why the PML-N-led government would not complete its five-year term, adding that the PPP had met opposition leaders solely on the speaker’s initiative.

“The PPP can meet opposition leaders as a political move, but the party has no mandate to do anything beyond that,” he added. To a question, Mr Chaudhry agreed that the PPP was creating difficulties for the government in its legislative business.

“The PPP is pinching us to make legislation, but it can’t keep itself away from the system,” he said.

He insisted that the opposition must join the parliamentary committee, as it would open the doors for consultation on other important national issues.

The minister said electoral reforms were necessary to prevent anyone from casting doubt on the elections. However, he did not elaborate on what kind of reforms the government intended to propose.

Published in Dawn, November 2nd, 2026

In a recent speech in the NA, PPP Chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari urged Mr Achakzai to use the “authority and power” delegated to him by jailed PTI founder Imran Khan to direct opposition members to participate in parliamentary committees and discuss pressing national issues.

He said that since parliament had decided, on a motion moved by the PPP, to constitute a committee on electoral reforms, the opposition leader should nominate a representative to the committee and submit their name to the speaker’s office.

Recalling that the opposition had described electoral rigging as its “fundamental issue”, he said, “If we make efforts to bring all stakeholders together in a committee or arrange a briefing on terrorism, economic, and security issues without the opposition’s participation, it will be pointless.”

Speaking to Dawn, PPP General Secretary Nayyar Bukhari said the party was not anticipating early elections; rather, efforts were being made to ensure transparent polls. He said it was the right time to initiate the electoral reform process because the government was about to complete three years of its five-year term. “In the final year of a five-year term, political parties usually launch their election campaigns and don’t concentrate on other issues. He added that alongside this concern, the PPP chairman genuinely wanted timely electoral reforms to make the country’s electoral process flawless, fair, and acceptable to all.

He agreed that it was the right time to launch the electoral reform process because political parties still had sufficient time to rectify the electoral system before the next general election.

He said it was a good initiative to take the opposition on board regarding electoral reforms, adding that the government and the opposition should also sit down together to appoint a new chief election commissioner, as the incumbent CEC, Sikandar Sultan Raja, remains in office despite his term expiring two years ago.

“I cannot understand why the leader of the opposition is not accepting the prime minister’s invitation to sit together for consultation on the new chief election commissioner,” he added.

He added that he would begin meeting parliamentary leaders of all parties from today (Monday) to invite them to join the committee on electoral reforms. The minister said there was no reason why the PML-N-led government would not complete its five-year term, adding that the PPP had met opposition leaders solely on the speaker’s initiative.

“The PPP can meet opposition leaders as a political move, but the party has no mandate to do anything beyond that,” he added. To a question, Mr Chaudhry agreed that the PPP was creating difficulties for the government in its legislative business.

“The PPP is pinching us to make legislation, but it can’t keep itself away from the system,” he said.

He insisted that the opposition must join the parliamentary committee, as it would open the doors for consultation on other important national issues.

The minister said electoral reforms were necessary to prevent anyone from casting doubt on the elections. However, he did not elaborate on what kind of reforms the government intended to propose.

headline: Looting, tear gas as youth anger spills over in Europe
description: Rioters loot stores in Frankfurt as protests sweep 34 German cities.
author: Agencies
article_text:
• Rioters loot stores in Frankfurt as protests sweep 34 German cities• Police clear housing camps in Lisbon• France opens attempted murder probe after petrol bomb attack on officers

FRANKFURT / PARIS / LISBON: Youth-led anger over living costs, housing and strained public services spilled onto streets across Europe over the weekend, bringing looting in Frankfurt, clashes in French cities and police raids on protest camps in Portugal.

The demonstrations in Germany were organised by the ‘Gen Z regelt’ (Gen Z takes charge) group, which says it opposes compulsory military service and wants greater investment in education as many young Germans struggle with rising costs.

Hooded rioters looted stores in Frankfurt late on Saturday night, after tens of thousands of demonstrators took to the streets across 34 cities, including Berlin and Munich.

In Germany’s financial hub, at least two stores were looted as protests turned violent, with several more damaged and police trying to get the situation under control. In Hamburg, some barricades had been set on fire.

German authorities said Saturday’s demonstrations, which coincide with Halloween festivities, had been largely peaceful, but warned of attempts by extremist groups to exploit the movement.

The German interior ministry alleged that parts of Germany’s far-left extremist scene and some groups linked to foreign extremist movements have joined efforts to mobilise support.

“We all have those images from France in our minds looting, burning houses, burning police vehicles, and attacks on police officers,” said Roman Poseck, interior minister for the state of Hesse, which includes Germany’s financial hub, Frankfurt.

“France must not be held up as a model in this regard.” Some businesses across German cities boarded up windows and planned early closures ahead of the demonstrations due to concerns over possible unrest, including along Berlin’s luxury Kurf­uerstendamm shopping boulevard.

Portugal

Police moved into Lisbon’s Rossio Square before dawn on Sunday to clear a camp of more than 50 tents pitched after thousands marched on Saturday against a rental bill.

After three warnings, dozens of officers, some with police dogs, dispersed hundreds of protesters using shields and some baton charges. A smaller camp in Porto was also dismantled.

Protesters want the minority centre-right government to scrap a bill that would make evictions easier and end rent caps on new leases. House prices in Portugal have more than doubled since 2017, and rents on new leases have nearly doubled, hitting young people especially hard.

Prime Minister Luis Montenegro has ruled out withdrawing the bill but said he is open to amendments before a final vote, while Socialist Party leader Jose Luis Carneiro urged talks with opposition parties and protesters.

France

Scuffles broke out in Paris and other cities after nationwide marches ended on the third weekend of protests since the riots and looting on Oct 17.

Riot police charged small groups in Paris and fired tear gas in Lyon and Toulouse, while tensions in Marseille eased by nightfall. Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said order had been maintained despite “a great deal of violence”.

Separately, French police have launched an attempted murder investigation after a petrol bomb was thrown at security forces during a weekend protest in Paris.

“Explosive devices were thrown at around fifteen gendarmes as well as police officers,” the prosecutor’s office said on Sunday.

No suspects “have been arrested at this stage in connection with the incident,” the prosecutor’s office said, adding that investigators were working to identify those responsible.

The movement began in late September with students angered by run-down schools, overcrowded classrooms and a university admissions system seen as unfair, and has since drawn in trade unions and a resurgent Yellow Vest movement.

Far-left leader Jean-Luc Melenchon headed the Paris march, while far-right leader Marine Le Pen leads polls ahead of April’s presidential election.

Published in Dawn, November 2nd, 2026

Hooded rioters looted stores in Frankfurt late on Saturday night, after tens of thousands of demonstrators took to the streets across 34 cities, including Berlin and Munich.

In Germany’s financial hub, at least two stores were looted as protests turned violent, with several more damaged and police trying to get the situation under control. In Hamburg, some barricades had been set on fire.

German authorities said Saturday’s demonstrations, which coincide with Halloween festivities, had been largely peaceful, but warned of attempts by extremist groups to exploit the movement.

The German interior ministry alleged that parts of Germany’s far-left extremist scene and some groups linked to foreign extremist movements have joined efforts to mobilise support.

“We all have those images from France in our minds looting, burning houses, burning police vehicles, and attacks on police officers,” said Roman Poseck, interior minister for the state of Hesse, which includes Germany’s financial hub, Frankfurt.

“France must not be held up as a model in this regard.” Some businesses across German cities boarded up windows and planned early closures ahead of the demonstrations due to concerns over possible unrest, including along Berlin’s luxury Kurf­uerstendamm shopping boulevard.

Portugal

Police moved into Lisbon’s Rossio Square before dawn on Sunday to clear a camp of more than 50 tents pitched after thousands marched on Saturday against a rental bill.

After three warnings, dozens of officers, some with police dogs, dispersed hundreds of protesters using shields and some baton charges. A smaller camp in Porto was also dismantled.

Protesters want the minority centre-right government to scrap a bill that would make evictions easier and end rent caps on new leases. House prices in Portugal have more than doubled since 2017, and rents on new leases have nearly doubled, hitting young people especially hard.

Prime Minister Luis Montenegro has ruled out withdrawing the bill but said he is open to amendments before a final vote, while Socialist Party leader Jose Luis Carneiro urged talks with opposition parties and protesters.

France

Scuffles broke out in Paris and other cities after nationwide marches ended on the third weekend of protests since the riots and looting on Oct 17.

Riot police charged small groups in Paris and fired tear gas in Lyon and Toulouse, while tensions in Marseille eased by nightfall. Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said order had been maintained despite “a great deal of violence”.

Separately, French police have launched an attempted murder investigation after a petrol bomb was thrown at security forces during a weekend protest in Paris.

“Explosive devices were thrown at around fifteen gendarmes as well as police officers,” the prosecutor’s office said on Sunday.

No suspects “have been arrested at this stage in connection with the incident,” the prosecutor’s office said, adding that investigators were working to identify those responsible.

The movement began in late September with students angered by run-down schools, overcrowded classrooms and a university admissions system seen as unfair, and has since drawn in trade unions and a resurgent Yellow Vest movement.

Far-left leader Jean-Luc Melenchon headed the Paris march, while far-right leader Marine Le Pen leads polls ahead of April’s presidential election.

headline: Without consequence
description: From drone attacks to online harassment and legal intimidation, the methods of silencing reporters are multiplying, with little fear of punishment.
author: Editorial
article_text:
JOURNALISTS today face ever more sophisticated threats, while those who target them continue to walk free. From drone attacks to online harassment and legal intimidation, the methods of silencing reporters are multiplying, with little fear of punishment.

This year’s International Day to End Impunity for Crimes against Journalists, observed today, carries the theme ‘Threats Evolve. Impunity Endures’.

According to Unesco, 189 journalists were killed in 2024 and 2025, most of them in conflict zones. Yet justice remains elusive in the vast majority of cases. The global impunity rate has risen to 86pc, the first increase since Unesco began measuring it in 2012. This failure to punish those responsible sends a dangerous message: journalists can be attacked or killed without fear of consequence.

Gaza shows what happens when those responsible are not held to account. The Committee to Protect Journalists recorded 129 journalists killed worldwide in 2025, with Israel responsible for two-thirds of the deaths. In August that year, Israeli strikes on Gaza’s Nasser Hospital killed 22 people, including five journalists. An AP investigation published a year later found that nobody had been held accountable.

For Palestinian journalists, who have been reporting a war largely closed to foreign media, the dangers are especially severe. Their deaths leave the outside world with fewer people able to document what is happening.

Similarly, in Sudan and Ukraine, journalists risk their lives exposing the horrors of war, while those who target them often escape justice. Without independent investigations and punishment for those found responsible, promises to protect journalists will remain empty.

Pakistan’s record is also deeply troubling. Freedom Network’s latest report documents threats and assaults against journalists, along with 45 cases of legal action or threatened prosecution. The growing use of Peca against journalists investigating official wrongdoing is particularly worrying. Repeated summonses, seized devices and costly court battles are enough to silence a reporter even without a conviction.

The human cost of this failure is evident in the case of journalist Mudassar Mahmood Naru. Eight years after his disappearance, his son is growing up without a father and his family is still waiting for answers.

The laws meant to protect journalists offer little comfort when the bodies responsible for enforcing them fail to act. In smaller towns, where reporters have fewer resources, intimidation often goes unreported.

The state must ensure that attacks are properly investigated, protection bodies function and cybercrime laws are not used to punish legitimate reporting. A country where journalists fear telling the truth more than wrongdoers fear being exposed has its priorities wrong.

Published in Dawn, November 2nd, 2026

article_html:
JOURNALISTS today face ever more sophisticated threats, while those who target them continue to walk free. From drone attacks to online harassment and legal intimidation, the methods of silencing reporters are multiplying, with little fear of punishment.

This year’s International Day to End Impunity for Crimes against Journalists, observed today, carries the theme ‘Threats Evolve. Impunity Endures’.

According to Unesco, 189 journalists were killed in 2024 and 2025, most of them in conflict zones. Yet justice remains elusive in the vast majority of cases. The global impunity rate has risen to 86pc, the first increase since Unesco began measuring it in 2012. This failure to punish those responsible sends a dangerous message: journalists can be attacked or killed without fear of consequence.

Gaza shows what happens when those responsible are not held to account. The Committee to Protect Journalists recorded 129 journalists killed worldwide in 2025, with Israel responsible for two-thirds of the deaths. In August that year, Israeli strikes on Gaza’s Nasser Hospital killed 22 people, including five journalists. An AP investigation published a year later found that nobody had been held accountable.

For Palestinian journalists, who have been reporting a war largely closed to foreign media, the dangers are especially severe. Their deaths leave the outside world with fewer people able to document what is happening.

Similarly, in Sudan and Ukraine, journalists risk their lives exposing the horrors of war, while those who target them often escape justice. Without independent investigations and punishment for those found responsible, promises to protect journalists will remain empty.

Pakistan’s record is also deeply troubling. Freedom Network’s latest report documents threats and assaults against journalists, along with 45 cases of legal action or threatened prosecution. The growing use of Peca against journalists investigating official wrongdoing is particularly worrying. Repeated summonses, seized devices and costly court battles are enough to silence a reporter even without a conviction.

The human cost of this failure is evident in the case of journalist Mudassar Mahmood Naru. Eight years after his disappearance, his son is growing up without a father and his family is still waiting for answers.

The laws meant to protect journalists offer little comfort when the bodies responsible for enforcing them fail to act. In smaller towns, where reporters have fewer resources, intimidation often goes unreported.

The state must ensure that attacks are properly investigated, protection bodies function and cybercrime laws are not used to punish legitimate reporting. A country where journalists fear telling the truth more than wrongdoers fear being exposed has its priorities wrong.

Published in Dawn, November 2nd, 2026

author: Editorial

headline: Two killed, one abducted in Balochistan's Qila Abdullah
description: Armed men flee to an undisclosed location after killing two people and abducting one.
author: Saleem Shahid
article_text:
QUETTA: Two people were killed while another was abducted by armed men in the Gulistan tehsil of Balochistan’s Qila Abdullah district on Sunday, officials said.

According to the officials, unidentified armed men abducted Haider, son of Bismillah. Local residents, angered by the kidnapping attempt, exchanged fire with the abductors. The exchange of fire between the residents and the kidnappers left two people dead. They were identified as Abdul Wali and Hanifullah.

After killing the two people and abducting Haider, the armed men fled to an undisclosed location.

Police and other law-enforcement agencies cordoned off the area and launched a search operation to recover the abducted man and arrest those involved in the incident.

Published in Dawn, November 2nd, 2026

headline: Karachi Port Trust handles ships with 101,000 tonnes of cargo
description: Two vessels bring 50,000 tonnes of DAP fertiliser and 51,000 tonnes of wheat.
author: Bakhtawar Mian
article_text:
ISLAMABAD: The Karachi Port Trust (KPT) has simultaneously handled two foreign bulk carriers carrying a combined 101,000 tonnes of diammonium phosphate (DAP) fertiliser and wheat.

Announcing the development on Sunday, Federal Minister for Maritime Affairs Muhammad Junaid Anwar Chaudhry said the concurrent unloading of the vessels underscored the port’s enhanced capacity to manage critical agricultural inputs and essential commodities efficiently.

The minister commended KPT engineers, port operators, pilots, the terminal operator, dockworkers and transporters for handling the vessels and maintaining cargo discharge operations.

He said the timely handling of essential imports was important for supporting agricultural production and ensuring food security.

The two vessels, MV ZHONG CHANG 538 and MV GOKOVA M, carrying 50,000 tonnes of DAP fertiliser and 51,000 tonnes of wheat, respectively, were berthed at Karachi Gateway Terminal Multipurpose.

Two vessels bring 50,000 tonnes of DAP fertiliser and 51,000 tonnes of wheat

Mr Chaudhry said the simultaneous handling of the vessels reflected KPT’s operational capacity and its efforts to improve berth utilisation, cargo-handling efficiency and supply chain performance.

‘Pursuing reforms’

He said the Ministry of Maritime Affairs was pursuing reforms to reduce vessel turnaround times, improve port management and strengthen maritime infrastructure to facilitate international trade and ensure an uninterrupted supply of essential commodities.

“Efficient port operations and streamlined logistics are essential for ensuring the timely movement of critical commodities and strengthening supply chains,” he added.

headline: A might-is-right world
description: Can distinct regional conflicts merge to push the world to the brink of a third world war?
author: Maleeha Lodhi
article_text:
THE world is passing through one of the most volatile periods in modern history. It is more unstable today than at any time since the end of the Cold War. The international system is fragmenting with rising big-power tensions. The old order with whatever rules it had is gone.

Power shifts continue to reshape the international landscape, marking the advent of a multipolar era. The disregard for international law and norms by big and regional powers has left countries having to navigate a rule-less terrain at a time of great uncertainty. Hard power has made a comeback. Powerful countries and regional powers are using military force or other coercive instruments to try to bend other states to their will. The threat or the use of force has become an option of first and not last resort, and the means to prevail over others.

These actions defy international law and global norms but continue with impunity. Diplomacy only happens after missiles have been fired.

Conflicts proliferate across the world — two major wars, between the US-Israel and Iran and between Ukraine and Russia as well as Israel’s genocidal war in Gaza and military actions against its neighbours.

There are a record number of conflicts today. A study by a Swedish university has counted the highest number of conflicts between states in 2025 since World War II. There are 65 active conflicts according to its data for last year. The risk of a global conflagration is also heightening.

Can this push the world to the brink of a third world war?

A new book seeks to answer this frequently raised question. War is Interested in You: The Breakdown of International Order and the Threat of World War Three by distinguished British columnist Gideon Rachman is an insightful book on a subject that is especially relevant today. He borrows the book’s title from Trotsky: “You may not be interested in war, but war is interested in you” — meaning war will come whether anyone wants it or is thinking about it.

Rachman identifies three fundamental reasons for the surge in conflicts and breakdown of international order. The first is the shifting global balance of power which is challenging US dominance. The second is the rise of what he calls ‘strongmen leaders’ who regard war as a necessary and legitimate tool to achieve their ends. The third is a consequence of the first two; as these trends take hold international rules and law are breaking down. “A law-governed world is giving way to a might-makes-right world,” he writes.

In explaining these causal factors, Rachman argues that the relative decline of the Western alliance and America’s retrenchment from its global role created an “opening” for “revisionist” powers dissatisfied with the present world order to take more risks. He cites Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and China’s more aggressive posture on Taiwan as cases in point. Trump’s use of military force against Iran, in defiance of international law and ignoring the views of its allies, has further contributed to the collapse of global order.

Can distinct regional conflicts merge to push the world to the brink of a third world war?

Greater international insecurity also stems from the emergence of a new generation of self-styled strongman leaders — Putin, Trump, Netanyahu — who deride the idea of a rules-based international order. Their acceptance of territorial annexation and belief in ‘might-makes-right’ has heightened the risk of international conflict.

Rachman suggests that both Trump and Putin subscribe to the “spheres of influence” theory, which they see as a more reliable guarantor of peace and stability than a rules-based order. The starkest expression of this, he asserts, is Trump’s revival of the Monroe doctrine for the Western Hemisphere.

In what Rachman characterises as a “might is right” world, growing global insecurity is driving up defence spending. Global rules and international institutions are being upended by strongman leaders, increasing the risk of more wars. While acts of war are the most dramatic examples of the breakdown of the rules-based order, Rachman argues that international institutions are crumbling in other ways too. Trump’s trade war and protectionist policies are, for example, accelerating this erosion.

Rachman examines today’s major wars and argues that while they have been distinct regional conflicts, they intersect at various points. But as these separate conflicts escalate, they risk eventually merging. His concept of an ‘axis of adversaries’ of the West or ‘axis of upheaval’ challenging the US-led world order greatly exaggerates the degree of cooperation between Russia, China, North Korea, and Iran whose interests are hardly identical. They may all want an end to US hegemony but that doesn’t make them partners in an alliance acting in unison.

The argument does not stand up to scrutiny. Rachman is unable to convincingly establish the “practical and ideological” links he posits between them. In fact, he himself acknowledges the limits of the Russian-Chinese partnership and strains among the four countries.

To the question of whether a conflict-ridden world is heading towards a global conflagration, Rachman’s answer is carefully qualified. A world war, he argues, would have two defining characteristics. One, the world’s major powers would have to be in direct conflict as they were in the First and Second World Wars. Two, the conflict would have to span continents. These conditions do not obtain today but they cannot be ruled out in the future.He sees a direct conflict between the US and China as the greatest risk.

Rachman devotes a chapter to last year’s conflict between India and Pakistan. It adds little to what has already been written about the military confrontation between the two nuclear neighbours. He sees the four-day conflict in May 2025 as a serious setback to India’s ambitions and efforts to de-hyphenate from Pakistan.

Among the lessons he draws from this episode is that “the risks of a very dangerous conflict in South Asia get too little attention compared to other global trouble spots”. He argues that the risk of future conflicts is heightened by the fact that both countries deployed increasingly sophisticated weapons during the crisis.

This is an intelligent book well worth reading for its sharp perspectives on war and peace even if one might disagree with some of the author’s assertions.

The writer is a former ambassador to the US, UK and UN.

headline: 100 women-led businesses featured at Quetta expo
description: Balochistan Board of Investment and Trade organises the event with the Trade Development Authority of Pakistan.
author: The Newspaper's Staff Correspondent
article_text:
QUETTA: About 100 women-led businesses showcased locally produced goods to buyers on Saturday at a two-day trade expo, where provincial officials pledged easier access to business loans and plans to triple exhibition capacity for future entrepreneurs.

The Women Entrepreneurs Expo (WEXNET) opened at the BUITEMS Expo Centre to connect local female founders directly with national and international markets. The Balochistan Board of Investment and Trade organised the event with the Trade Development Authority of Pakistan.

Rubaba Buledi, adviser to the Balochistan chief minister on women’s development, inaugurated the exhibition and announced plans to expand the showcase from 100 stalls to 300 in its next edition.

“The Women Development Department will play an active role in supporting women-led businesses, facilitating financial assistance and access to loans, and addressing the challenges faced by women entrepreneurs,” Buledi said.

Bilal Khan Kakar, vice chairman of the provincial investment board, said the initiative has the full backing of Chief Minister Mir Sarfraz Bugti and Federal Minister Jam Kamal Khan to help women build commercial linkages and achieve economic self-reliance.

Shehryar Taj, secretary of the trade authority, said WEXNET has held about 12 exhibitions nationwide since 2000 to link female entrepreneurs with new buyers.

headline: Unified crypto industry body proposed
description: Asia Web3 Alliance Japan president says the country’s growing cryptocurrency market faces significant challenges in the absence of verified investor data.
author: Khaleeq Kiani
article_text:
ISLAMABAD: In the wake of a recent multibillion-dollar cybersecurity breach involving Binance, Pakistan needs a unified industry representative body to safeguard digital asset investors and impr­ove coordination with inte­r­national cryptocurrency exchanges, Asia Web3 Alliance Japan (AWAJ) President Hinza Asif said.

In a statement, Ms Asif said the country’s growing cryptocurrency market faced significant challenges in the absence of verified investor data and an organised mechanism to represent industry stakeholders, particularly in the event of major cybersecurity or financial incidents involving international exchanges.

She pointed out that Pakistan ranked third in the 2025 Global Crypto Adoption Index compiled by Chainalysis. Estimates suggesting around 40 million crypto-linked accounts and digital asset exposure of between $10 billion and $20bn indicated the potential scale of the market, although these figures had not been officially verified as representing individual investors.

Referring to the cybersecurity incident involving Binance, Ms Asif said breaches at major exchanges could result in financial losses, unauthorised transactions and disruptions to withdrawals, potentially undermining investor confidence.

She added that the incident’s potential impact on Pakistani investors rem­ained unclear and requ­ired independent verification.

“The question is who will represent and protect Pakistani investors if an international exchange faces a major cybersecurity or financial crisis,” she said, adding that the country lacked an established mechanism to coordinate investor complaints and engage with international exchanges in such circumstances.

Welcoming the government’s regulatory initiatives through the Pakistan Virtual Assets Regulatory Authority (PVARA), she said the regulator and an independent industry association would have complementary roles.

While PVARA would oversee regulatory matters within its legal mandate, an industry representative body could provide a platform for fintech compan­ies, blockchain businesses, technology professionals and investors to raise concerns and engage with policymakers, she said.

Ms Asif also called for the establishment of a national digital finance platform supported by reliable market research, coordinated investor grievance mechanisms, cybersecurity awareness and formal partnerships with international industry organisations.

She said Pakistan’s digital finance potential extended beyond cryptocurrency trading to include blockchain applications, digital payments, fintech entrepreneurship and international investment.

headline: Human trafficking attempt in Balochistan's Panjgur foiled
description: Official says security forces would continue to maintain a strict vigil and carry out operations to curb human trafficking.
author: Behram Baloch
article_text:
GWADAR: Security forces have thwarted a human trafficking attempt in the Paroom area of Panjgur district, arresting 173 undocumented Afghan nationals.

Official sources said that a large number of Afghan nationals, driven by economic and social hardships as well as other factors in Afghanistan, fall prey to human traffickers in an attempt to travel to Iran, Turkiye and European countries via Pakistan.

An official said that security forces would continue to maintain a strict vigil and carry out operations to curb human trafficking.

He added that all the arrested Afghan nationals would be handed over to the police for further legal action.

Published in Dawn, November 2nd, 2026

headline: Gilgit-Baltistan celebrates 79 years of independence
description: Morning flag-hoisting ceremony held at the historic Chinar Bagh in Gilgit.
author: Jamil Nagri
article_text:
GILGIT: The 79th Independence Day of Gilgit-Baltistan (GB) was celebrated across the region on Sunday with traditional zeal and fervour, marked by military parades, cultural festivities, polo competitions and tributes to the heroes who liberated the homeland from Dogra rule.

On Nov 1, 1947, the GB Scouts liberated the region from the Dogra Raj and raised the flag of freedom, declaring an independent state that later joined Pakistan.

Government buildings were decorated with Pakistani flags. People from all walks of life wearing traditional dresses participated in events held in all 10 districts of GB to mark the day.

A morning flag-hoisting ceremony was held at the historic Chinar Bagh in Gilgit, attended by Governor Syed Mehdi Shah, Chief Minister Amjad Hussain, Force Commander GB Maj Gen Tajdeed Mumtaz, ministers, elected representatives, and civil and military officials.

The governor, chief minister and force commander laid floral wreaths at the martyrs’ memorial and offered Fatiha, while a contingent of police and GB Scouts presented a salute.

At the Pakistan Army helipad in Gilgit, contingents from Pakistan Army, Northern Light Infantry Centre, GB Scouts, Women Police and GB Police participated in the parade. Paragliding performances and local sports competitions enthralled participants, while youngsters danced to national songs.

In his address, GB CM Amjad Hussain said Nov 1 is a glorious day in GB’s history when brave ancestors liberated the region from the Dogra Raj and showed their affiliation with Pakistan’s ideology. “The independence demands from us to remember the enduring sacrifices of our forefathers and to renew our commitment to realising their dreams,” he said. “Today, it is our responsibility to transform the spirit of freedom into a force for progress, prosperity, peace, justice and public service.”

Separately, President Asif Ali Zardari and Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif extended heartfelt felicitations to the people of GB and paid tribute to those who took part in the historic struggle, Radio Pakistan reported.

Also, Inter-Services Public Relations released a special song paying tribute to the brave sons of GB. Produced entirely by local artists, the song features poetry by Zeeshan Mehdi and vocals by JJ Ali Shina from Skardu, celebrating the region’s heritage and deep-rooted love for Pakistan.

Published in Dawn, November 2nd, 2026

headline: Pyramid of pain
description: Defined by the FBI as “violent nihilistic extremism”, 764 promotes harm for the sake of harm; they are the engagement farmers of evil.
author: Zarrar Khuhro
article_text:
WHAT is the common thread in all these cases?

In 2026, a 14-year-old girl in Pakistan tortures and kills her pet cat, sending the pictures of the abuse to an unknown person for approval. In late 2024 in Stockholm, a 14-year-old boy walks up to a man in his 80s, stabs him repeatedly in the back and flees, taking nothing from his victim except blood. Another teenager in the same country tries to coerce a 13-year-old to take his own life and video-stream his suicide. In the US state of Oregon, a 16-year-old shoots and kills three students and a teacher at an elementary school before being shot dead. A year earlier, in the same state, a 14-year-old was arrested for planning a mass shooting/ suicide at a mall. WHAT is the common thread in all these cases?

In 2026, a 14-year-old girl in Pakistan tortures and kills her pet cat, sending the pictures of the abuse to an unknown person for approval. In late 2024 in Stockholm, a 14-year-old boy walks up to a man in his 80s, stabs him repeatedly in the back and flees, taking nothing from his victim except blood. Another teenager in the same country tries to coerce a 13-year-old to take his own life and video-stream his suicide. In the US state of Oregon, a 16-year-old shoots and kills three students and a teacher at an elementary school before being shot dead. A year earlier, in the same state, a 14-year-old was arrested for planning a mass shooting/ suicide at a mall. In June 2026, a school shooting takes place in the Philippines where two suspects, aged 14 and 15, killed three students and wounded 20 others.

In all these cases, the driving force for this kind of torture, self-harm, murder, and suicide is a shadowy online group called 764 that is dedicated to the ‘gamification’ of violence, in which your online status rises in proportion to the harm you can do — to yourself or, preferably, to others.

764 takes its name from the first three digits of the zip code for Stephenville, Texas, the home of its founder Bradley Cadenhead, known online as Felix, who created this group in 2021 when he was 15. While he is now serving 80 years in a US prison after being convicted of possessing child sexual abuse material, his network not only survives, but is considered a tier-1 security threat in the US, alongside the likes of Al Qaeda and IS, and — as evidence of its transnational reach and decentralised nature — is also listed as a terrorist group in New Zealand and Canada, to name just two.

But what sets 764 apart from ‘mainstream’ terrorist groups is its ideology, or lack thereof. There’s no political agenda, barring perhaps a shared hatred for humanity, a desire to dismantle morality as a whole, and to accelerate, as some of its adherents put it, the destruction of society. Defined by the FBI as “violent nihilistic extremism”, it promotes harm for the sake of harm; they are the engagement farmers of evil.

The hunt for victims begins on social media pages frequented by young people or the chat servers of otherwise perfectly innocent games like Minecraft and Roblox, and then shifts onto Discord servers or Telegram. With a predator’s instinct, they target the young, the vulnerable, and as forensic psychologist Joni Johnston puts it, the “sad and the strange”.

Once suitable targets are identified, a well-thought-out process of psychological manipulation, extortion, and coercion begins in which victims often turn into perpetrators who can then rise in the ranks depending on how many others they can coerce or blackmail into committing atrocities.

The 764 group and the larger networks it is affiliated with even publish grooming and blackmail guides and digital scrapbooks (‘lorebooks’ in their parlance) of their exploits, not only gaining them further clout and respect in their twisted system of merit but also serving as ‘how-to’ guides for new recruits.

They are the engagement farmers of evil.

The initial approach is cloaked in kindness; from there, it often turns into romantic overtures intended to gain the victim’s trust. Once compromising pictures of and personal information on the victim are obtained, they are used to blackmail the victims into acts like progressively harming themselves, their pets, or other human beings. Typical ‘tasks’ and ‘challenges’ entail cutting the 764 logo into one’s arm or writing the online nickname of one’s ‘controller’ in blood and then sending photographic evidence to the group. The deeper they get, the more they are threatened with exposure by the 764 group.

Once control has been established, the victims are made to victimise others and commit serious crimes, much like a pyramid scheme of pain.

In the US alone, 764 has been linked to at least five mass shootings. Its founder didn’t invent the grooming method he and his followers use; he borrowed it from already existing groups like CVLT and Greggy’s Cult, which specialised in coercing children to expose themselves sexually or harm themselves. Cadenhead had come across these groups when he was 10 and was sent real footage of people being tortured while on a Minecraft server.

764 is only one part of a much larger network known as ‘The Com’ which is short for ‘Community’, and shares this status with other accelerationist, neo-Nazi, and openly satanic sub-groups such as No Lives Matter, Satanic Front, and Maniacs Murder Club.

In one sense, the rise of such groups is a sign of the depths to which society has sunk, where traditional morality is to be mocked and self-gratification is the greatest good. And in these murky deeps, there are sharks.

headline: Wage board set as unrest shuts Bangladesh garment factories
description: The dispute has raised concerns about widespread disruption to an industry that employs about four million workers.
author: Reuters
article_text:
DHAKA: Bangladesh said on Sunday it had set up a wage board to review garment workers’ pay and urged employees to return to work as violent protests forced the closure of more than 500 factories, with police firing tear gas and water cannon at demonstrators.

The dispute has raised concerns about widespread disruption to an industry that employs about four million workers, generates more than 80pc of Bangladesh’s export earnings and supplies clothing to many leading Western brands.

The workers in the South Asian nation are demanding a minimum monthly wage of 30,000 taka ($245), more than double the current 12,500 taka, saying rising costs of food, housing, transport and healthcare have sharply eroded their purchasing power.

“The cost of living has increased far beyond our incomes,” worker Mahin Hossain said. “After paying rent, there is very little left for food, our children’s education and other essential expenses. Many are finding it almost impossible to support their families.”

Police use tear gas

Despite the announcement of the wage board, thousands of garment workers staged demonstrations on Sunday, blocking roads in Dhaka and Gazipur, outside the capital, and disrupting transport across key industrial areas.

Police used tear gas and water cannon to disperse protesters after demonstrators threw bricks at officers, and a police vehicle and a police box were set on fire in separate incidents. Authorities deployed Border Guard Bangladesh personnel to maintain order.

The latest unrest follows demonstrations in Ashulia, a major garment manufacturing hub on the outskirts of Dhaka, where dozens of factories suspended operations on Saturday after workers staged protests demanding higher pay.

In all, the unrest has forced 529 garment factories to shut down and left 987,190 workers out of work across the country’s main industrial hubs, according to the Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association.

Labour and Employment Minister Ariful Haque Choudhury said the wage board was formed after discussions with workers’ representatives and industry leaders, and urged workers to resume work.

The six-member wage board comprises two representatives each from workers and employers, along with a government representative and a neutral member. The body has been tasked with reviewing wages in the garment sector and recommending revised pay rates.

Delayed shipments

Choudhury warned that prolonged disruptions could delay export shipments and payments from international buyers, creating further difficulties for manufacturers and workers alike. Bangladesh’s ready-made garment industry, the world’s largest after China, contributes about 10pc of gross domestic product and is the backbone of the economy.

Manufacturers, however, say the sector is facing mounting challenges, including rising production costs, periodic gas and electricity shortages, and uncertainty in energy markets linked to tensions in the Middle East.

article_html:
DHAKA: Bangladesh said on Sunday it had set up a wage board to review garment workers’ pay and urged employees to return to work as violent protests forced the closure of more than 500 factories, with police firing tear gas and water cannon at demonstrators.

The dispute has raised concerns about widespread disruption to an industry that employs about four million workers, generates more than 80pc of Bangladesh’s export earnings and supplies clothing to many leading Western brands.

The workers in the South Asian nation are demanding a minimum monthly wage of 30,000 taka ($245), more than double the current 12,500 taka, saying rising costs of food, housing, transport and healthcare have sharply eroded their purchasing power.

“The cost of living has increased far beyond our incomes,” worker Mahin Hossain said. “After paying rent, there is very little left for food, our children’s education and other essential expenses. Many are finding it almost impossible to support their families.”

Police use tear gas

Despite the announcement of the wage board, thousands of garment workers staged demonstrations on Sunday, blocking roads in Dhaka and Gazipur, outside the capital, and disrupting transport across key industrial areas.

Police used tear gas and water cannon to disperse protesters after demonstrators threw bricks at officers, and a police vehicle and a police box were set on fire in separate incidents. Authorities deployed Border Guard Bangladesh personnel to maintain order.

The latest unrest follows demonstrations in Ashulia, a major garment manufacturing hub on the outskirts of Dhaka, where dozens of factories suspended operations on Saturday after workers staged protests demanding higher pay.

In all, the unrest has forced 529 garment factories to shut down and left 987,190 workers out of work across the country’s main industrial hubs, according to the Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association.

Labour and Employment Minister Ariful Haque Choudhury said the wage board was formed after discussions with workers’ representatives and industry leaders, and urged workers to resume work.

The six-member wage board comprises two representatives each from workers and employers, along with a government representative and a neutral member. The body has been tasked with reviewing wages in the garment sector and recommending revised pay rates.

Delayed shipments

Choudhury warned that prolonged disruptions could delay export shipments and payments from international buyers, creating further difficulties for manufacturers and workers alike. Bangladesh’s ready-made garment industry, the world’s largest after China, contributes about 10pc of gross domestic product and is the backbone of the economy.

Manufacturers, however, say the sector is facing mounting challenges, including rising production costs, periodic gas and electricity shortages, and uncertainty in energy markets linked to tensions in the Middle East.

headline: BRICS accelerates green transition
description: The key question is how many of these activities will be put into practice and how many will remain on paper only.
author: ANN, China Daily
article_text:
THE BRICS countries are united by the collective goal of combating climate change. As BRICS membership has expanded, so has the potential for the BRICS countries to contribute to the global green transition. This is especially true regarding climate finance and technology, where the BRICS collectively possess deep capacities.

Recent international challenges have strengthened the case for BRICS cooperation. According to the OECD, the United States’ aid cuts resulted in the largest ever decline in foreign aid on record in 2025, while growth in global climate finance lost momentum. In June, the World Bank scrapped its target requiring 45pc of its financing to produce climate co-benefits, a move widely tied to US pressure.

That makes practical South-South cooperation a necessity in global green finance and technology. The BRICS-founded New Development Bank provides the institutional basis for mobilising resources, with a solid pipeline of projects. The NDB took shape while BRICS countries were simultaneously negotiating the Paris Agreement. The bank became fully operational in 2016 — the year the Paris Agreement entered into force. This means that unlike earlier development banks, the NDB was designed when climate was already a top global concern. This enabled members to embed green finance into the NDB from day one. The treaty establishing the NDB — the bank’s supreme legal instrument — tasks it with mobilising resources “for infrastructure and sustainable development projects”.

What this means for climate finance is spelled out in plans and policies. The NDB’s 2022-26 general strategy targets 40pc of financing to be approved for climate mitigation and adaptation. The same strategy rules out financing any new coal-fired power capacity. The NDB approved $5.59 billion in climate finance during 2022-25, representing 44pc of total financing over the period and beating its own 40pc target during this period.

While these activities are similar to those of other development banks, the NDB has engaged in legal experimentation that reflects its nature as an institution wholly owned by emerging economies and developing countries. Its green debt framework, while designed to align with the global benchmark Green Bond Principles and broadly consistent with the sustainable finance taxonomy of the European Union, also leaves scope to issue bonds aligned with the standards of individual BRICS members.

The bank has also pursued local currency financing to reduce foreign exchange and other risks to borrowers. Its first green bond was denominated in the renminbi and was the first green bond issued by an international institution in China’s domestic market. In 2025, local currency financing accounted for about 46pc of new project approvals, a record share, mainly in renminbi, rand and rupee. Overall, 29.3pc of all NDB financing was in the currencies of bank members by the end of 2025. However, the vast majority of the NDB portfolio remains denominated in US dollars.

After a decade of operations, the NDB has established itself as a growing source of climate finance. With the expanding of membership, the bank’s strategy during the next five-year period is likely to continue to target greater financing in member currencies while strengthening focus on technologies.

However, the NDB’s impact is constrained by the bank’s scale. Since inception, the NDB has approved almost $43 billion by early 2026 across all projects. That is meaningful for the Global South, but scaling the BRICS contribution to climate action requires direct cooperation among the BRICS members.

The members of the grouping recently started to explore the potential for closer climate cooperation within BRICS frameworks, welcoming a memorandum of understanding on a BRICS Carbon Market Partnership in 2024. In 2025, the BRICS leaders endorsed a broad climate leadership agenda and adopted a cooperation framework for climate finance.

In addition to potential cooperation on a BRICS Carbon Markets Partnership to share expertise, build capacity and link carbon markets with climate finance, the framework identified potential to develop a catalogue of national sustainable finance taxonomies to identify areas of convergence, while also considering promotion of “interoperability” of different approaches.

This activity to promote cross-border green finance flows could draw lessons from the EU-China (later joined by Singapore) common ground taxonomy and ASEAN’s sustainable finance taxonomy. There are also positive signs for greater cooperation between the NDB and national development finance institutions.

Another 2025 document proposed options for enhancing BRICS cooperation on climate tech, including setting up a BRICS climate “patent pool”, as one of several non-binding models, alongside humanitarian and open-licensing proposals, to widen access to climate-related technologies.

The key question is how many of these activities will be put into practice and how many will remain on paper only. The voluntary, non-legally binding format of BRICS cooperation provides flexibility but can also mean limited clarity about how to implement plans and assess results.

Finally, BRICS climate action could be strengthened through deeper engagement with the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change institutions and other development banks. Following the BRICS leaders’ call on multilateral development banks to enhance collaboration with climate funds, the NDB could explore partnership agreements with the Green Climate Fund and the Adaptation Fund. The NDB could also build on its initial engagement with the UNFCCC’s technology transfer body, the Climate Technology Centre & Network, to develop a pipeline of de-risked climate-tech projects.

While the NDB already participates in the Multilateral Development Bank climate action group, with common methodologies and joint reporting, it has engaged in little joint lending with other MDBs, unlike the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank. Greater co-financing would be another way to stretch the NDB’s resources.

Following next month’s APEC meeting in Shenzhen, attention in China will turn to China’s chairing of BRICS in 2027. The opportunity will be to build out the BRICS contribution to an evolving ecosystem of climate action standards and financing.

Achieving this would turn ambitious ideas into concrete cooperation while strengthening links with other key sources of finance and tech capacity.

Published in Dawn, November 2nd, 2026

That is meaningful for the Global South, but scaling the BRICS contribution to climate action requires direct cooperation among the BRICS members.

The members of the grouping recently started to explore the potential for closer climate cooperation within BRICS frameworks, welcoming a memorandum of understanding on a BRICS Carbon Market Partnership in 2024. In 2025, the BRICS leaders endorsed a broad climate leadership agenda and adopted a cooperation framework for climate finance.

In addition to potential cooperation on a BRICS Carbon Markets Partnership to share expertise, build capacity and link carbon markets with climate finance, the framework identified potential to develop a catalogue of national sustainable finance taxonomies to identify areas of convergence, while also considering promotion of “interoperability” of different approaches.

This activity to promote cross-border green finance flows could draw lessons from the EU-China (later joined by Singapore) common ground taxonomy and ASEAN’s sustainable finance taxonomy. There are also positive signs for greater cooperation between the NDB and national development finance institutions.

Another 2025 document proposed options for enhancing BRICS cooperation on climate tech, including setting up a BRICS climate “patent pool”, as one of several non-binding models, alongside humanitarian and open-licensing proposals, to widen access to climate-related technologies.

The key question is how many of these activities will be put into practice and how many will remain on paper only. The voluntary, non-legally binding format of BRICS cooperation provides flexibility but can also mean limited clarity about how to implement plans and assess results.

Finally, BRICS climate action could be strengthened through deeper engagement with the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change institutions and other development banks. Following the BRICS leaders’ call on multilateral development banks to enhance collaboration with climate funds, the NDB could explore partnership agreements with the Green Climate Fund and the Adaptation Fund. While the NDB already participates in the Multilateral Development Bank climate action group, with common methodologies and joint reporting, it has engaged in little joint lending with other MDBs, unlike the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank. Greater co-financing would be another way to stretch the NDB’s resources.

Following next month’s APEC meeting in Shenzhen, attention in China will turn to China’s chairing of BRICS in 2027. The opportunity will be to build out the BRICS contribution to an evolving ecosystem of climate action standards and financing.

Achieving this would turn ambitious ideas into concrete cooperation while strengthening links with other key sources of finance and tech capacity.

headline: Illegal house allotment, compensation payment: Peeda Act proceedings against former Auqaf secretary ordered
description: The order, issued under the Punjab Employees Efficiency, Discipline and Accountability Act 2006, accuses the BS-20 officer of abusing his authority.
author: Mansoor Malik
article_text:
LAHORE: The Punjab government has ordered disciplinary proceedings against the former secretary/chief administrator of Auqaf department, Dr Tahir Raza Bukhari, for his alleged role in the illegal allotment of a government-reserved Khateeb’s residence to a private person and subsequent payment of Rs8.162 million in compensation to that individual against the government property, affected by Neela Gumbad project.

The order, issued under the Punjab Employees Efficiency, Discipline and Accountability (Peeda) Act 2006, accuses the BS-20 officer of abusing his authority by facilitating the illegal allotment of Unit-54, a house reserved for the Khateeb of Jamia Masjid, Neela Gumbad, to one Shahid Ishaq, son of retired provincial Khateeb Mufti Muhammad Ishaq Saqi, in Dec 2023 despite knowing the house’s reserved status and that it could not be allotted to any private person.

Dr Bukhari allegedly pressured field officers to submit favourable reports and later concealed material facts during high-level official meetings, ultimately resulting in a massive financial loss of Rs8.162m to the exchequer as compensation was paid out against the state property.

Ordering initiation of disciplinary proceedings against the accused under the Peeda Act 2006, the Punjab chief minister, acting as competent authority, appointed Punjab Planning and Development Board (P&DB) Chairman Dr Naeem Rauf as inquiry officer to proceed against the accused officer in terms of Section 5(1)(b) read with Section 9 of the Act ibid.

The inquiry officer has been asked to submit his report and recommendations to the Auqaf department secretary within 60 days of the initiation of inquiry.

The order says an application was submitted by a private person, Shahid Ishaq, son of Mr Ishaq Saqi (ex-provincial Khateeb) to the Auqaf secretary/chief administrator on Dec 19, 2023, for allotment of the house (Unit 54) attached to Jamia Masjid, Neela Gumbad, which was actually reserved for Khateeb of the mosque. At that time too, the house was under illegal occupation of Ishaq Saqi, who was residing there even after his retirement on April 1, 2019.

Instead of calling the report based on facts, the order says, Dr Bukhari pressurised the zonal administrator of Auqaf, Lahore (West), to submit a report in the favour of the applicant by writing the comments: “Hasb-e-Istada Karwai ho” in spite of having knowledge that no Khateeb house could be allotted to any private person, which is tantamount to corruption, inefficiency and misconduct under the provisions of Peeda Act 2006.

The order says, on the accused officer’s direction, the Lahore ex-zonal administrator submitted his report in favour of this illegal allotment on Dec 23, 2023. With active connivance of field officers– manager circle 2, Lahore, and zonal administrator, Lahore West – the former secretary, who was in close contact with Mufti Ishaq Saqi, allotted the reserved house illegally to a private person on Dec 28, 2023, the order says.

As per the order, the former secretary’s representative, Khalid Mehmood Sandhu, ex-director (Estate), attended a meeting, chaired by the then Local Govt and Community Development (LG&CD) department secretary, regarding payment of compensation to the affected persons of Neela Gumbad project on Aug 29, 2025. However, Mr Sandhu deliberately did not mention during the meeting that compensation of the said house could not be made to the illegal allottee, for it being a reserved house.

“Minutes of the 29th meeting of Provincial Cabinet held on Oct 06, 2025, transpire vide para 102.5 and 102.6 that you deliberately did not mention there that compensation of the said house cannot be made to the illegal allottee,” the order says.

Besides allotting the house illegally, the former secretary also caused a huge loss of Rs8.162m to the exchequer, as the amount was paid as compensation for the house to Shahid Ishaq, which is tantamount to corruption, inefficiency and misconduct under the Peeda Act, 2006.

The government has asked the accused former secretary to submit his written defence to the inquiry officer within seven days of the date of receipt of this order.

As both Dr Bukhari and Khalid Sandhu are also accused of financial irregularities in public funds, the order recommends recovery of around Rs34m from them.

After approval of the chief secretary, Senior Member Board of Revenue (SMBR) Nabeel Javed, in April 2026, was entrusted with the task to conduct a probe into the allegations against the two officers.

Earlier, responding to a Dawn query about the status of the probe against the two officers, Mr Javed had said it was “in process”.

Meanwhile, the Auqaf department has appointed Deputy Director (Admin) Azeem Hayat as departmental representative, allowing the accused officers to consult the record on which the aforesaid charges are based, if he desires so, within seven days of the receipt of the order.

Published in Dawn, November 2nd, 2026
