article_html:
Newlands, Cape Town. Saturday morning, before the first ball.

Marnus Labuschagne crouches on his haunches at the edge of the outfield, waiting to bat. Australia need 288 to win the Test and the series. In the first innings he made a five-ball duck. He has scored 11 Test hundreds, and the last came at Old Trafford in July 2023. For a stretch he was the best batter in the world.

He stands, walks to the middle, and takes guard. He will face three balls. I have not stopped thinking about them.

Nothing moved me, so I wrote nothing. Somebody has to move a writer to write…

Part One: The Wait

Chapter One: Moved

Some months earlier

I write about this game only when it moves me. Good cricket does not count. Good cricket arrives every week and asks nothing of you. Being moved is rarer: a stranger does something you did not know a person could do, in a country you may never see, at an hour when you should be asleep, and for a few minutes you stop being an audience and become a witness. The first Test of the Ashes did that to me, in two days, and I wrote about it. I watched the other four to the last ball. Then the series ended, an English summer came and went, and I could not name you one innings. Nothing moved me, so I wrote nothing. Somebody has to move a writer to write, and the universe, with its usual disregard for my sleep, took the job. My resistance lasted about one session.

Chapter Two: Two Rooms

Same city. Same Saturday night

In the first room, a performer who has done this show 200 times walks onto a stage built for it. The lighting is rehearsed. The song you came for arrives second, exactly where it was promised. The audience paid for that, and it is delivered to the minute. Nobody leaves disappointed and nobody leaves changed. This is entertainment, and I have nothing against it. Its virtue is that it keeps its word.

In the second room, a band walks out with sketches and no plan. In the spring of 1959 Miles Davis brought his musicians into a studio with little more than a handful of scales and melodic outlines, and what they made became the best-selling jazz record of all time. It could have been a mess. The patron in that room knows it could have been a mess, because he has sat through the nights when it was. He pays for the chance to find out.

The two audiences differ in more than taste. The first judges the evening against a promise. The second judges himself against the evening: was I paying enough attention to be there when it happened? Entertainment asks whether you enjoyed it. Art asks whether you were awake.

Test cricket is the second room, stretched to five days.

Part Two: The Match

Chapter Three: Tuesday

Newlands, day one

The series stands at one all. Australia won in Durban by 214, on Matt Renshaw’s 190. South Africa won in Gqeberha by an innings and 31 runs, on Temba Bavuma’s 179. Cape Town decides it.

Pat Cummins wins the toss and chooses to field, citing moisture in the pitch. A captain has made that choice at Newlands only 12 times since 1889. The moisture turns out to be a rumour. By lunch Marques Ackerman and Aiden Markram have South Africa at 140 without loss.

Ackerman is playing his second Test. He makes 95 off 94 balls, with twelve fours and two sixes, four of the fours in a row off Mitchell Starc. Then, five runs short of a hundred, he walks down the pitch to Nathan Lyon, who has waited 15 years for that look on a batter’s face. Stumped. Afterward Ackerman says he lives by the sword and dies by it, and that he left a hundred out there. He does not pretend to be happy about it.

Then Starc.

There is a kind of bowler around whom an afternoon changes ownership. Wasim Akram is one. Shane Warne was another. The scoreboard was never the evidence. The evidence was the batter, who knew first. On Tuesday evening Starc joins them. He has Bedingham caught on 50 and, two balls later, Wiaan Mulder, caught behind for a duck. He takes Rickelton and Jansen in a single over with the new ball, then Coetzee and Rabada. South Africa fall from 203 for 1 to 329 all out. Starc finishes with six for 72, his 20th five-wicket haul, and he is not done.

Mulder walks off with a zero beside his name. Keep that number.

In the last half hour of the day Starc is bowling himself off his feet, and at the start of his 22nd over he reaches down for his right calf and runs in anyway.

Chapter Four: Wednesday

Day two

Simon Harmer has Travis Head chopping on for 41. Then Labuschagne, going back to a ball that wanted him forward, edges it to slip, where Aiden Markram takes the catch. Five balls. No runs. He arrived at Newlands needing a score to keep his place, and Australia are 58 for 2.

Tuesday, Mulder: nought. Wednesday, Labuschagne: nought. The match sets them side by side and says nothing.

I am travelling, and the Test starts at an hour that my body, wherever it thinks it is, cannot place. By the second night I have moved two meetings. By the fourth I have moved the rest. I, who could not spare 10 minutes for cricket since the Ashes, now discover that I have five days.

Chapter Five: Friday

Day four

Thursday belongs to Australia. Josh Inglis makes 102 off 135 balls and, with Alex Carey, who makes 80, adds 185. Australia lead by 100. By the close South Africa are four down and 40 ahead, a lead you could carry in one hand.

Friday belongs to two men who have known each other since school. Ryan Rickelton already owns a Test double century and is still the quieter name in a batting order that includes Aiden Markram and Temba Bavuma. Mulder walked off on Tuesday with a zero.

Their plan is a lesson in humility. Rickelton has decided to take a few on the body rather than play the short ball, and he does. He spends 37 balls in the 90s. On 92, Starc bangs one in short, Rickelton shoulders arms, and it thuds into his ribs. He lifts his shirt to show Travis Head, at short leg, the bruise coming up, for confirmation or approval. Head, by all accounts, offers both.

Rickelton reaches his hundred after tea and finishes on 101 off 219 balls. Then Mulder reverse-sweeps, Josh Inglis dives at backward point to cut it off, and Rickelton is run out, the stumps broken by Labuschagne. The stand is worth 154.

It would be easier to say that Mulder rescued South Africa. What he does is odder. He rescues himself, and South Africa happens to be standing next to him. He makes 115 off 221 balls, and on the stroke of stumps he clubs Cummins to deep midwicket, where Mitchell Starc, who has done everything else on this ground for three days, takes the catch. South Africa have 387. Australia need 288.

Wiaan Mulder. Tuesday: 0. Friday: 115.

The same 387 would have been a decent total on Tuesday. On Friday, on a pitch that has begun to come apart, from a side that was four down the night before, it is a verdict.

Nothing else in sport asks you to be brave slowly, and then makes you wait through the night to learn whether it counted.

Chapter Six: Saturday Morning

Day five

Kagiso Rabada has the new ball. Travis Head takes a single off the second delivery. The third is down the leg side, Matt Renshaw, the hero of Durban, is strangled, and Rickelton takes the catch behind the stumps. A golden duck. Labuschagne gets up off his haunches and walks out.

David Warner had predicted that the day would end with Labuschagne a 100 not out and Australia winning with seven wickets down.

The first ball Marnus faces runs off the leading edge, past gully, for four. Two balls later Rabada bowls one that nips back. Labuschagne, playing no shot, is hit on the back pad in front of the stumps. Richard Kettleborough raises his finger. Labuschagne reviews. The replay shows the ball clipping the off bail, which makes it umpire’s call, and the original decision stands. Out for four. 5-2.

Umpire’s call is a rule written for doubt. If the ball is only clipping the stump, the umpire’s original decision stands, whatever it was. Had Kettleborough shaken his head, the very same replay would have left Labuschagne standing where he was.

I have thought about the innings that follows that headshake more than I have thought about most of the ones that were played. It starts the way his best always have, quietly: a leave, a leave, a punch through cover that sounds like a door closing on a bad year.

By lunch he is on 30, and Australia, three down, are breathing again. By tea the drought is over. By the close it is a hundred, and Warner’s forecast, which sounded absurd that morning, looks like prophecy. It never happened. I would swear I watched it.

This is what faith costs in Test cricket, and what luck pays out. Everything Labuschagne has done since he was a boy, the dawn nets, the leaves, the belief, is weighed in the end against a sliver of bail and one man’s reading of it.

Luck is not the opposite of skill in this game. It is the second signature on the contract. A batter can prepare for everything except the sliver, and the sliver is where Test cricket keeps its mystery.

I wrote once about Virat Kohli and the fifth stump, that line outside off where a ball extends an invitation and a great batter accepts it against his own training.

Kohli was beaten by the ball he should have left. Labuschagne was beaten by the ball he left. The craft is the same and so is the verdict: the sport does not care how well you prepared. I support South Africa. I have rarely been so sorry to see them succeed.

By the end of the day Nathan Lyon, at number 10, will have made 33 not out, the top score of the innings, 29 more than a man who was once the best batter in the world.

Labuschagne has the application, the talent, the faith and the hours. All of it is still there. And one morning, for no reason anyone can name, it leaves, the way a word does when you say it too many times and it becomes a sound. He may have played his last Test for Australia in that over. I hope not.

Marnus Labuschagne. Wednesday: 0. Saturday: 4.

Head scores the way a vending machine dispenses: promptly, correctly, and without looking at you. He hits a few boundaries, then edges Rabada to Marco Jansen at gully. 14. It is Rabada’s 350th Test wicket, reached in 13,808 balls, faster than any bowler in history and 911 balls quicker than Dale Steyn. I am alarmed by how much I enjoy it.

Simon Harmer comes on in the 12th over, and the morning comes apart. Inglis is run out for four after Cameron Green sets off for a run that was never on, and Ackerman, who left a hundred on the field on Tuesday, takes a wicket back from silly point.

Alex Carey reverse-sweeps and top-edges to Jansen. Cooper Connolly is caught behind for nought. Starc, promoted to number eight to deal with the footmarks, survives 25 balls without scoring and is caught at bat-pad off the last ball before lunch, the longest duck of his Test career. At lunch Australia are 60 for 7. Harmer has 3-5 from eight overs.

Chapter Seven: Saturday Afternoon

Day five, after lunch.

After lunch the match stops moving, and it becomes the best thing in it. Australia score two runs in an hour. There is a stretch of 78 balls without a run. Green is sheltered from Harmer’s off breaks, and Cummins, who has come out beside him with a plan to bat time instead of runs, defends everything that comes.

Six fielders crouch around the bat. It is a standoff in which the only weapon anyone holds is patience. When the first run finally comes, the Newlands crowd cheers it, ironically and at length. Then Harmer changes ends, drags one through Green’s gate, and Green is bowled for 27. 62-8.

And then two men who have no business being dangerous become dangerous. Cummins faces 90 balls and scores 11 runs, and I have never been prouder of a ratio. Nathan Lyon, who bowled 44 overs in South Africa’s second innings, bats as though that were a warm-up. They add 45. The result was settled hours ago. They know it, the crowd knows it, and everyone awake across the world knows it. They stay anyway.

This is the strange, magnificent design of the thing. A Test match asks the athlete to bring his best courage and his best stamina not for an hour but for five days. Then, on the fifth afternoon, when the specialists have failed, it hands the match to the people who were hired to do something else.

A fast bowler walks out and decides to become a wall. A spinner decides to become a clock. Nothing they do will change the result, and that is exactly why it matters. A win is a fact. This is a gift.

When a man spends 90 balls on something that cannot be won, the scoreboard stops being the point, and the rest of us find out what valour looks like once the reward has been taken away.

Just before tea Harmer traps Cummins lbw. Cummins reviews. The ball is clipping the off bail, and the umpire’s call stands. It is the second time that day those words have decided a man’s fate, and both times the call goes South Africa’s way.

Every great Test victory owes something to luck. Then, with the first ball of his 22nd over, Harmer bowls Josh Hazlewood. Australia are all out for 111. South Africa win by 176.

Harmer finishes with 6 for 16 from 21.1 overs, 14 of them maidens, and 10 wickets in the match, the first time he has done that in a Test. He is 37. He bowled through a torn nail on Thursday. He spent years with Essex in English county cricket, was recalled, and on a Saturday in Cape Town takes apart the top-ranked Test side in the world.

Part Three: The Vigil

Chapter Eight: Everyone Awake

Some hours later.

A machine can give you the result of this Test in one line. It will be correct, and it will take four seconds. Australia 111, South Africa by 176, the series 2-1.

It cannot tell you what it was like to be awake for it.

We are living through a strange subtraction. Answers arrive before the questions are finished. Summaries sit above the thing they summarise. Almost everything that once cost an afternoon now costs a tap, and the cost was never the enemy.

The cost was where the meaning was kept. A letter mattered because it took a week. A song mattered because you had to wait for the radio to play it. Take away the wait and you take away the room where the feeling lived.

Test cricket is the last large public thing built so that nothing can be skipped. You cannot fast-forward the 90th ball. You cannot be told how it felt. The only way to know is to stay, and staying is the whole price of admission, paid in the oldest currency we have: hours, spent in company.

Somewhere in that fifth afternoon, in a time zone that had no business being awake, a stranger was watching Cummins defend a ball for a reason no efficiency expert would accept. Most of us had no stake in the result. We were there because the sport asks a very human question, which is whether you will stay.

That is human-centred design. The game is built to the scale of a person. It takes five days because a person needs five days to become who he will be on the fifth. It lets a man fail in public and return in the second innings.

It makes 10 team-mates watch each member be afraid, one at a time, and know exactly what it costs. And in an age that can produce the likeness of almost anything, it offers the one thing that cannot be produced: a reason to stay up with strangers for something that may not end well, and to be glad you did.

Chapter Nine: Thank You

16 months earlier, and also now.

In June 2025 I sat at Lord’s through Rabada’s third-innings spell of the World Test Championship final and watched Bavuma lift the mace. It was South Africa’s first global title in 27 years, and it was the day and the occasion that moved me most that year.

That same summer I wrote about a five-Test series and called the piece Five Shades of Flat. Now the same South Africans, under Bavuma, who lost the first Test of this series and won the next two, are the number one Test side in the world for the first time since January 2016.

Thank you Test Cricket..

Thank you For lunch, to begin with, which stops a Test match at its most dangerous moment so that twenty-two men can have a civilized meal.

For tea, the second truce of the day.

For the maiden over, the only unit of achievement in sport defined by nothing happening.

For the duck, a zero named after a bird, so that even the worst day a batter can have arrives with a little feathered mercy.

For a game in which a man can score eleven in ninety balls and be remembered as a hero, and another can score four in three balls and be mourned.

For umpire’s call, in which a machine admits it is not sure.

For the nightwatchman, the bad light, the follow-on, the draw that feels like a victory and the victory that feels like a funeral.

We could not have invented you. No committee would have approved you. You take five days to say what other sports say in two hours, and you say it better, because you leave room for people to be wrong in public and the time for them to come back.

I closed the laptop. The room was quiet, and the quiet was full, the way a house is after the guests have gone. Whether Marnus Labuschagne walks out again for Australia is the one thing this match left unanswered. Test cricket will answer in its own time. I intend to be awake when it does.

Yours, awake.. I suspect he is too.

Newlands, Cape Town. Saturday morning, before the first ball.

Marnus Labuschagne crouches on his haunches at the edge of the outfield, waiting to bat. Australia need 288 to win the Test and the series. In the first innings he made a five-ball duck. He has scored 11 Test hundreds, and the last came at Old Trafford in July 2023. For a stretch he was the best batter in the world.

He stands, walks to the middle, and takes guard. He will face three balls. I have not stopped thinking about them.

Nothing moved me, so I wrote nothing. Somebody has to move a writer to write…

Chapter One: Moved

Some months earlier

I write about this game only when it moves me. Good cricket does not count. Good cricket arrives every week and asks nothing of you. Being moved is rarer: a stranger does something you did not know a person could do, in a country you may never see, at an hour when you should be asleep, and for a few minutes you stop being an audience and become a witness. The first Test of the Ashes did that to me, in two days, and I wrote about it. I watched the other four to the last ball. Then the series ended, an English summer came and went, and I could not name you one innings. Nothing moved me, so I wrote nothing. Somebody has to move a writer to write, and the universe, with its usual disregard for my sleep, took the job. My resistance lasted about one session.

Chapter Two: Two Rooms

Same city. Same Saturday night

In the first room, a performer who has done this show 200 times walks onto a stage built for it. The lighting is rehearsed. The song you came for arrives second, exactly where it was promised. The audience paid for that, and it is delivered to the minute. Nobody leaves disappointed and nobody leaves changed. This is entertainment, and I have nothing against it. Its virtue is that it keeps its word.

In the second room, a band walks out with sketches and no plan. In the spring of 1959 Miles Davis brought his musicians into a studio with little more than a handful of scales and melodic outlines, and what they made became the best-selling jazz record of all time. It could have been a mess. The patron in that room knows it could have been a mess, because he has sat through the nights when it was. He pays for the chance to find out.

The two audiences differ in more than taste. The first judges the evening against a promise. The second judges himself against the evening: was I paying enough attention to be there when it happened? Entertainment asks whether you enjoyed it. Art asks whether you were awake.

Test cricket is the second room, stretched to five days.

Chapter Three: Tuesday

Newlands, day one

The series stands at one all. Australia won in Durban by 214, on Matt Renshaw’s 190. South Africa won in Gqeberha by an innings and 31 runs, on Temba Bavuma’s 179. Cape Town decides it.

Pat Cummins wins the toss and chooses to field, citing moisture in the pitch. A captain has made that choice at Newlands only 12 times since 1889. The moisture turns out to be a rumour. By lunch Marques Ackerman and Aiden Markram have South Africa at 140 without loss.

Ackerman is playing his second Test. He makes 95 off 94 balls, with twelve fours and two sixes, four of the fours in a row off Mitchell Starc. Then, five runs short of a hundred, he walks down the pitch to Nathan Lyon, who has waited 15 years for that look on a batter’s face. Stumped. Afterward Ackerman says he lives by the sword and dies by it, and that he left a hundred out there. He does not pretend to be happy about it.

Then Starc.

There is a kind of bowler around whom an afternoon changes ownership. Wasim Akram is one. Shane Warne was another. The scoreboard was never the evidence. The evidence was the batter, who knew first. On Tuesday evening Starc joins them. He has Bedingham caught on 50 and, two balls later, Wiaan Mulder, caught behind for a duck. He takes Rickelton and Jansen in a single over with the new ball, then Coetzee and Rabada. South Africa fall from 203 for 1 to 329 all out. Starc finishes with six for 72, his 20th five-wicket haul, and he is not done.

Mulder walks off with a zero beside his name. Keep that number.

In the last half hour of the day Starc is bowling himself off his feet, and at the start of his 22nd over he reaches down for his right calf and runs in anyway.

Chapter Four: Wednesday

Day two

Simon Harmer has Travis Head chopping on for 41. Then Labuschagne, going back to a ball that wanted him forward, edges it to slip, where Aiden Markram takes the catch. Five balls. No runs. He arrived at Newlands needing a score to keep his place, and Australia are 58 for 2.

Tuesday, Mulder: nought. Wednesday, Labuschagne: nought. The match sets them side by side and says nothing.

I am travelling, and the Test starts at an hour that my body, wherever it thinks it is, cannot place. By the second night I have moved two meetings. By the fourth I have moved the rest. I, who could not spare 10 minutes for cricket since the Ashes, now discover that I have five days.

Chapter Five: Friday

Day four

Thursday belongs to Australia. Josh Inglis makes 102 off 135 balls and, with Alex Carey, who makes 80, adds 185. Australia lead by 100. By the close South Africa are four down and 40 ahead, a lead you could carry in one hand.

Friday belongs to two men who have known each other since school. Ryan Rickelton already owns a Test double century and is still the quieter name in a batting order that includes Aiden Markram and Temba Bavuma. Mulder walked off on Tuesday with a zero.

Their plan is a lesson in humility. Rickelton has decided to take a few on the body rather than play the short ball, and he does. He spends 37 balls in the 90s. On 92, Starc bangs one in short, Rickelton shoulders arms, and it thuds into his ribs. He lifts his shirt to show Travis Head, at short leg, the bruise coming up, for confirmation or approval. Head, by all accounts, offers both.

Rickelton reaches his hundred after tea and finishes on 101 off 219 balls. Then Mulder reverse-sweeps, Josh Inglis dives at backward point to cut it off, and Rickelton is run out, the stumps broken by Labuschagne. The stand is worth 154.

It would be easier to say that Mulder rescued South Africa. What he does is odder. He rescues himself, and South Africa happens to be standing next to him. He makes 115 off 221 balls, and on the stroke of stumps he clubs Cummins to deep midwicket, where Mitchell Starc, who has done everything else on this ground for three days, takes the catch. South Africa have 387. Australia need 288.

Wiaan Mulder. Tuesday: 0. Friday: 115.

The same 387 would have been a decent total on Tuesday. On Friday, on a pitch that has begun to come apart, from a side that was four down the night before, it is a verdict.

Nothing else in sport asks you to be brave slowly, and then makes you wait through the night to learn whether it counted.

Chapter Six: Saturday Morning

Day five

Kagiso Rabada has the new ball. Travis Head takes a single off the second delivery. The third is down the leg side, Matt Renshaw, the hero of Durban, is strangled, and Rickelton takes the catch behind the stumps. A golden duck. Labuschagne gets up off his haunches and walks out.

David Warner had predicted that the day would end with Labuschagne a 100 not out and Australia winning with seven wickets down.

The first ball Marnus faces runs off the leading edge, past gully, for four. Two balls later Rabada bowls one that nips back. Labuschagne, playing no shot, is hit on the back pad in front of the stumps. Richard Kettleborough raises his finger. Labuschagne reviews. The replay shows the ball clipping the off bail, which makes it umpire’s call, and the original decision stands. Out for four. 5-2.

Umpire’s call is a rule written for doubt. If the ball is only clipping the stump, the umpire’s original decision stands, whatever it was. Had Kettleborough shaken his head, the very same replay would have left Labuschagne standing where he was.

I have thought about the innings that follows that headshake more than I have thought about most of the ones that were played. It starts the way his best always have, quietly: a leave, a leave, a punch through cover that sounds like a door closing on a bad year.

By lunch he is on 30, and Australia, three down, are breathing again. By tea the drought is over. By the close it is a hundred, and Warner’s forecast, which sounded absurd that morning, looks like prophecy. It never happened. I would swear I watched it.

This is what faith costs in Test cricket, and what luck pays out. Everything Labuschagne has done since he was a boy, the dawn nets, the leaves, the belief, is weighed in the end against a sliver of bail and one man’s reading of it.

Luck is not the opposite of skill in this game. It is the second signature on the contract. A batter can prepare for everything except the sliver, and the sliver is where Test cricket keeps its mystery.

I wrote once about Virat Kohli and the fifth stump, that line outside off where a ball extends an invitation and a great batter accepts it against his own training.

Kohli was beaten by the ball he should have left. Labuschagne was beaten by the ball he left. The craft is the same and so is the verdict: the sport does not care how well you prepared. I support South Africa. I have rarely been so sorry to see them succeed.

By the end of the day Nathan Lyon, at number 10, will have made 33 not out, the top score of the innings, 29 more than a man who was once the best batter in the world.

Labuschagne has the application, the talent, the faith and the hours. All of it is still there. And one morning, for no reason anyone can name, it leaves, the way a word does when you say it too many times and it becomes a sound. He may have played his last Test for Australia in that over. I hope not.

Marnus Labuschagne. Wednesday: 0. Saturday: 4.

Head scores the way a vending machine dispenses: promptly, correctly, and without looking at you. He hits a few boundaries, then edges Rabada to Marco Jansen at gully. 14. It is Rabada’s 350th Test wicket, reached in 13,808 balls, faster than any bowler in history and 911 balls quicker than Dale Steyn. I am alarmed by how much I enjoy it.

Simon Harmer comes on in the 12th over, and the morning comes apart. Inglis is run out for four after Cameron Green sets off for a run that was never on, and Ackerman, who left a hundred on the field on Tuesday, takes a wicket back from silly point.

Alex Carey reverse-sweeps and top-edges to Jansen. Cooper Connolly is caught behind for nought. Starc, promoted to number eight to deal with the footmarks, survives 25 balls without scoring and is caught at bat-pad off the last ball before lunch, the longest duck of his Test career. At lunch Australia are 60 for 7. Harmer has 3-5 from eight overs.

Chapter Seven: Saturday Afternoon

Day five, after lunch.

After lunch the match stops moving, and it becomes the best thing in it. Australia score two runs in an hour. There is a stretch of 78 balls without a run. Green is sheltered from Harmer’s off breaks, and Cummins, who has come out beside him with a plan to bat time instead of runs, defends everything that comes.

Six fielders crouch around the bat. It is a standoff in which the only weapon anyone holds is patience. When the first run finally comes, the Newlands crowd cheers it, ironically and at length. Then Harmer changes ends, drags one through Green’s gate, and Green is bowled for 27. 62-8.

And then two men who have no business being dangerous become dangerous. Cummins faces 90 balls and scores 11 runs, and I have never been prouder of a ratio. Nathan Lyon, who bowled 44 overs in South Africa’s second innings, bats as though that were a warm-up. They add 45. The result was settled hours ago. They know it, the crowd knows it, and everyone awake across the world knows it. They stay anyway.

This is the strange, magnificent design of the thing. A Test match asks the athlete to bring his best courage and his best stamina not for an hour but for five days. Then, on the fifth afternoon, when the specialists have failed, it hands the match to the people who were hired to do something else.

A fast bowler walks out and decides to become a wall. A spinner decides to become a clock. Nothing they do will change the result, and that is exactly why it matters. A win is a fact. This is a gift.

When a man spends 90 balls on something that cannot be won, the scoreboard stops being the point, and the rest of us find out what valour looks like once the reward has been taken away.

Just before tea Harmer traps Cummins lbw. Cummins reviews. The ball is clipping the off bail, and the umpire’s call stands. It is the second time that day those words have decided a man’s fate, and both times the call goes South Africa’s way.

Every great Test victory owes something to luck. Then, with the first ball of his 22nd over, Harmer bowls Josh Hazlewood. Australia are all out for 111. South Africa win by 176.

Harmer finishes with 6 for 16 from 21.1 overs, 14 of them maidens, and 10 wickets in the match, the first time he has done that in a Test. He is 37. He bowled through a torn nail on Thursday. He spent years with Essex in English county cricket, was recalled, and on a Saturday in Cape Town takes apart the top-ranked Test side in the world.

Chapter Eight: Everyone Awake

Some hours later.

A machine can give you the result of this Test in one line. It will be correct, and it will take four seconds. Australia 111, South Africa by 176, the series 2-1.

It cannot tell you what it was like to be awake for it.

We are living through a strange subtraction. Answers arrive before the questions are finished. Summaries sit above the thing they summarise. Almost everything that once cost an afternoon now costs a tap, and the cost was never the enemy.

The cost was where the meaning was kept. A letter mattered because it took a week. A song mattered because you had to wait for the radio to play it. Take away the wait and you take away the room where the feeling lived.

Test cricket is the last large public thing built so that nothing can be skipped. You cannot fast-forward the 90th ball. You cannot be told how it felt. The only way to know is to stay, and staying is the whole price of admission, paid in the oldest currency we have: hours, spent in company.

Somewhere in that fifth afternoon, in a time zone that had no business being awake, a stranger was watching Cummins defend a ball for a reason no efficiency expert would accept. Most of us had no stake in the result. We were there because the sport asks a very human question, which is whether you will stay.

That is human-centred design. The game is built to the scale of a person. It takes five days because a person needs five days to become who he will be on the fifth. It lets a man fail in public and return in the second innings.

It makes 10 team-mates watch each member be afraid, one at a time, and know exactly what it costs. And in an age that can produce the likeness of almost anything, it offers the one thing that cannot be produced: a reason to stay up with strangers for something that may not end well, and to be glad you did.

Chapter Nine: Thank You

16 months earlier, and also now.

In June 2025 I sat at Lord’s through Rabada’s third-innings spell of the World Test Championship final and watched Bavuma lift the mace. It was South Africa’s first global title in 27 years, and it was the day and the occasion that moved me most that year.

That same summer I wrote about a five-Test series and called the piece Five Shades of Flat. Now the same South Africans, under Bavuma, who lost the first Test of this series and won the next two, are the number one Test side in the world for the first time since January 2016.

Thank you Test Cricket..

Thank you For lunch, to begin with, which stops a Test match at its most dangerous moment so that twenty-two men can have a civilized meal.

For tea, the second truce of the day.

For the maiden over, the only unit of achievement in sport defined by nothing happening.

For the duck, a zero named after a bird, so that even the worst day a batter can have arrives with a little feathered mercy.

For a game in which a man can score eleven in ninety balls and be remembered as a hero, and another can score four in three balls and be mourned.

For umpire’s call, in which a machine admits it is not sure.

For the nightwatchman, the bad light, the follow-on, the draw that feels like a victory and the victory that feels like a funeral.

We could not have invented you. No committee would have approved you. You take five days to say what other sports say in two hours, and you say it better, because you leave room for people to be wrong in public and the time for them to come back.

I closed the laptop. The room was quiet, and the quiet was full, the way a house is after the guests have gone. Whether Marnus Labuschagne walks out again for Australia is the one thing this match left unanswered. Test cricket will answer in its own time. I intend to be awake when it does.

Yours, awake.. I suspect he is too.

That same summer I wrote about a five-Test series and called the piece Five Shades of Flat. Now the same South Africans, under Bavuma, who lost the first Test of this series and won the next two, are the number one Test side in the world for the first time since January 2016.
Thank you Test Cricket..
Thank you For lunch, to begin with, which stops a Test match at its most dangerous moment so that twenty-two men can have a civilized meal.
For tea, the second truce of the day.
For the maiden over, the only unit of achievement in sport defined by nothing happening.
For the duck, a zero named after a bird, so that even the worst day a batter can have arrives with a little feathered mercy.
For a game in which a man can score eleven in ninety balls and be remembered as a hero, and another can score four in three balls and be mourned.
For umpire’s call, in which a machine admits it is not sure.
For the nightwatchman, the bad light, the follow-on, the draw that feels like a victory and the victory that feels like a funeral.

We could not have invented you. No committee would have approved you. You take five days to say what other sports say in two hours, and you say it better, because you leave room for people to be wrong in public and the time for them to come back.

I closed the laptop. The room was quiet, and the quiet was full, the way a house is after the guests have gone. Whether Marnus Labuschagne walks out again for Australia is the one thing this match left unanswered. Test cricket will answer in its own time. I intend to be awake when it does.
Yours, awake.. I suspect he is too.

headline: Kuwait lifts oil output to highest since start of Iran war, source says
description: Kuwait raised its crude oil production to 2.1 million barrels per day in October, the highest level since the...
article_text:
Kuwait raised its crude oil production to 2.1 million barrels per day in October, the highest level since the outbreak of the Iran war and a rise of over 300,000 bpd from September, a person with direct knowledge of the matter told Reuters.

The increase came despite a record number of attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, adding to signs that Gulf oil producers are maintaining or increasing output as they adapt to the disruption risks.

The person asked not to be named because they were not authorised to speak publicly about Kuwaiti production.

headline: LHC directs jail authorities to arrange meeting between Noreen Niazi, her daughters
description: Directive comes after Noreen was shifted to the Punjab Institute of Cardiology following her deteriorating health.
author: Wajih Ahmad Sheikh
article_text:
LAHORE: The Lahore High Court (LHC) on Monday directed jail authorities to arrange a meeting between Noreen Niazi, the sister of PTI founder Imran Khan, and her two daughters on Tuesday (tomorrow).

Justice Abher Gul Khan issued the directives while hearing petitions challenging the extensions in the detention orders of Imran’s sisters Noreen, Uzma Khan and Aleema Khanum.

The judge also summoned the Lahore deputy commissioner to appear in person on Nov 4 and explain the extensions in the detention orders of Noreen and Uzma Khan.

Aleema and Noreen, along with their sister Uzma Khan, were detained under the Punjab Maintenance of Public Order Ordinance, 1960 in September, as the PTI geared up for a protest march to Islamabad. Their detentions have come amid reports of several PTI leaders and workers being taken into custody ahead of the march planned to demand Imran’s release from prison.

Among them, Aleema was detained on Sept 20 for 30 days and Noreen and Uzma the next day for the same period. Their detention was challenged in the court after the 30-day period lapsed last month, following which the Punjab government informed the court that their detention periods had been extended for another 30 days.

During Monday’s hearing, the petitioners’ counsel Rana Mudassar Umar told the court that Noreen’s two daughters and lawyers wanted to meet her. He expressed concern over her health, saying she was an elderly woman and her actual condition could only be ascertained after meeting her.

Among the three detainees, Noreen had been shifted to the Punjab Institute of Cardiology (PIC) following her deteriorating health, on the recommendation of the doctors of the Kot Lakhpat Jail, where she has been detained. Later, adviser to the prime minister on political affairs, Rana Sanaullah, had informed the Senate that Noreen was fine after being provided medical treatment in Lahore.

On Monday, the judge asked a provincial law officer whether a specific day had been fixed for prisoners’ meetings. The law officer said the jail authorities had no objection to allowing the meeting.

The law officer also submitted a report on behalf of the Home Department, stating that Noreen had been taken to hospital for treatment and subsequently shifted back to jail on doctors’ advice. He said her daughter, Hajira Niazi, had been allowed to meet her at the hospital on Oct 29.

The court subsequently directed the jail authorities to facilitate a meeting between Noreen and her two daughters on Tuesday.

Meanwhile, the judge adjourned the hearing of a petition challenging Aleema’s fresh detention until next week.

Reports sought

Earlier in the day, the LHC had sought reports from the Punjab Home Department. Justice Khan directed the Home Department to submit the reports by 2pm as she heard pleas filed by Noreen’s daughter, Sakeena, and Shahrez Khan, Aleema’s son.

The petitioner’s counsel contended that Aleema, Noreen and Uzma’s detentions had been extended “unlawfully”. He noted that after the initial 30-day detention period, the Lahore deputy commissioner had issued a notification for its extension.

He claimed that the detained women had also not been allowed to meet their family members or lawyers.

The counsel asked the court to declare the fresh detention notifications “illegal”.

PTI Secretary General Advocate Salman Akram Raja informed the court that Aleema’s driver had also been detained. He requested the court to show leniency towards the driver, saying his family was deeply distressed.

Justice Khan then sought reports from the provincial Home Department and said she would examine the matter after going through the reports.

headline: UAE to protect energy infrastructure, invest in new export routes to prepare for Iran war, minister says
description: The UAE will protect its energy infrastructure and invest in new export routes, storage capacity abroad and shipping...
article_text:
The UAE will protect its energy infrastructure and invest in new export routes, storage capacity abroad and shipping fleets to be better prepared for the US-Israeli war on Iran, its energy minister said, Reuters reports.

Minister Suhail al-Mazrouei said the course of the war could not be predicted, but the UAE would be more prepared than before.

The UAE has been exporting crude via Fujairah, which sits just outside the Strait of Hormuz. It is building a new pipeline to Fujairah that will double crude capacity by next year.

headline: On eve of midterms, final polls point to Democratic gains, but can Republicans hold the Senate?
description: The prospect of Democratic gains is no longer being acknowledged only by Democratic strategists or traditionally liberal media outlets.
author: Anwar Iqbal
article_text:
Democrats have made significant gains in the final days of the 2026 midterm campaign, with new polls showing them leading in several states that President Donald Trump carried in 2024. The findings point to a changing political landscape, although the outcome of the Senate contests remains uncertain.

The final New York Times/Siena College surveys of seven key Senate battlegrounds show Democratic candidates ahead in Michigan, Texas, Kansas, Maine and Ohio. They also hold narrower leads in Alaska and Iowa, where the contests remain highly competitive.

The results have attracted particular attention because several of these states have traditionally favoured Republicans. Democratic leads in Texas and Kansas, in particular, would have appeared unlikely only a few months ago.

The surveys, released on November 1, covered 5,708 likely voters across the seven states. The individual state surveys had margins of sampling error ranging from approximately 3.3 to 4.8 percentage points.

In Michigan, Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed leads Republican Mike Rogers by 53 to 42 per cent. In Texas, James Talarico is ahead of Republican Ken Paxton, 50 to 43pc.

Kansas Democrat Adam Hamilton leads incumbent Republican Senator Roger Marshall, 49 to 44pc, while in Maine, Democrat Troy Jackson leads Republican Senator Susan Collins, 51 to 45pc.

Ohio presents another potentially significant contest. Former Democratic senator Sherrod Brown leads Republican Jon Husted, 49 to 44pc.

The margins are narrower in Alaska and Iowa. Mary Peltola leads Republican Senator Dan Sullivan, 48 to 46pc, while Democrat Josh Turek is ahead of Republican Ashley Hinson, 48 to 47pc.

Although Democrats lead numerically in all seven surveys, the differences in Alaska and Iowa are too small to establish a statistically reliable advantage. Even the larger leads elsewhere remain subject to polling error.

The findings nevertheless show how competitive the Senate map has become as both parties seek control of Congress.

A Republican warning: The Senate remains competitive

The prospect of Democratic gains is no longer being acknowledged only by Democratic strategists or traditionally liberal media outlets. Fox News, which generally offers a more favourable perspective on Republican electoral prospects, has also revised its assessments.

In its November 1 Power Rankings, Fox moved Kansas from “Lean Republican” to “Toss-up”, acknowledging that the Republican incumbent was facing a serious challenge in a traditionally conservative state.

Of the 100 seats in the Senate, Fox considers Democrats favoured in 48 Senate seats and Republicans in 45, with seven competitive states likely to determine control of the chamber. It nevertheless describes the overall Senate contest as a toss-up.

Its reasoning is based largely on electoral geography.

Trump carried seven of the 11 battleground states in 2024, several by double-digit margins. Republicans believe that voters who supported him in those states could return to the polls and support Republican Senate candidates, even if the national political environment has shifted.

Fox also points to the number of undecided voters in Alaska, Iowa and Kansas. A late movement towards Republican candidates, combined with strong Election Day participation, could change the outcome.

The network’s analysis presents two possible scenarios: a Democratic gain that could give the party as many as 55 Senate seats, or a Republican performance strong enough to preserve a majority of up to 52. Either party needs to secure 51 seats in the Senate for a majority win.

The House picture is different. Fox’s final Power Rankings project that Democrats are likely to win at least 223 seats, with the possibility of reaching 240 in a strong performance. In the lower House of Representatives, the winner needs to gain at least 218 out of the 435 voting seats.

Other forecasts examine the changing political map.

The Wall Street Journal, reporting on the latest assessment by the Cook Political Report, said Democrats had become slight favourites to capture the Senate.

Cook identifies seven Senate races — Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Michigan, Ohio and Texas — as sufficiently competitive to remain within the margin of error.

For the House, Cook projects Democratic gains of between 12 and 25 seats, potentially giving the party a majority of as many as 240 members.

CBS News has also reported a sustained Democratic advantage in its House modelling. Its October 25 analysis, however, offered an important qualification: the Democratic lead had remained relatively stable rather than expanding, and voters who were still uncertain about participating tended to lean more Republican.

That distinction matters. A favourable polling environment does not necessarily mean that all voters expressing dissatisfaction with the administration will turn out on Election Day.

The Harvard model assigns probabilities to a possible Democratic takeover.

A forecast from the Harvard ElectIt project offers another way of assessing the congressional contests. The project provides three versions of its 2026 forecast: one based on its statistical election model, a second incorporating national generic-ballot polling and a third incorporating available state and district polls.

The underlying LogisTiCC model uses historical congressional election results and accounts for factors including incumbency, candidate-specific effects, strategic departures from office and the historical tendency of the president’s party to lose ground in midterm elections. The poll-based versions adjust the model using additional polling information.

Under the forecast configuration displayed in the Harvard link used for this report, Democrats have a 96pc probability of taking the House and a 79pc probability of gaining control of the Senate.

The model projects approximately 241 Democratic House seats, a net gain of 26, and 53 Democratic Senate seats, an increase of six.

The reported 95pc ranges are wide: 214 to 282 seats in the House and 47 to 57 in the Senate. These ranges underline that the figures are statistical estimates, not guaranteed outcomes.

The Senate projection is particularly significant because it illustrates how the model evaluates the possibility of Democrats overcoming the geographical disadvantages that have traditionally made the chamber difficult for them to capture.

The Harvard project cautions against treating a single projected seat count as a certain result. Its different forecast versions can produce different estimates as polling information changes.

Progressive politics and the changing Democratic coalition

The emerging political picture also reflects a longer evolution within the Democratic Party, particularly the growth of progressive politics and dissatisfaction with established political institutions.

Commentator Zeeshan Shah, a physician in Northern Virginia, believes Senator Bernie Sanders helped inject new energy into the progressive movement, creating political space for candidates challenging the Republican establishment.

After Sanders came New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who is believed to have taken that energy into the mainstream by directly challenging Trump and the politics associated with his administration, according to Mohsin Masood, a Virginia educationist.

Political science professor Farhat Haq believes Democrats could benefit from another pendulum swing in American politics, driven largely by dissatisfaction with Trump.

She points to rising living costs, the war involving Iran and the Gaza conflict as factors contributing to public discontent. Haq links the economic consequences of the Iran war to inflation and the pressure on household budgets.

She also argues that Trump has lost support among some of the groups that helped him politically, including Latino voters. Haq notes that PTI supporters in the United States, despite remaining politically active, are no longer supporting Trump as they did previously.

Together, these assessments suggest that the political shift may reflect more than the immediate circumstances of the campaign. Economic anxiety, foreign-policy disagreements and disappointment with established political leadership have all entered the debate over the direction of the country.

The final test comes on Tuesday

Republicans currently hold a 53-47 Senate majority, including two independents who caucus with Democrats. Democrats need a net gain of four seats to secure an outright 51-seat majority.

The House is a more straightforward target. Republicans hold a narrow majority, and the latest polling and election ratings point to a highly competitive contest for control.

A change in either chamber would significantly affect Trump’s ability to advance his legislative programme. Democratic control would also give the opposition party greater authority to investigate the administration and scrutinise its policies.

The final polls and forecasts show Democrats entering Election Day with opportunities in several states and congressional districts that were not widely expected to be competitive earlier in the campaign.

Yet polling error cannot be dismissed. Undecided voters, differences in turnout and the difficulty of predicting who will actually vote can all produce results that diverge from final surveys.

For Democrats, the election offers an opportunity to regain the House and potentially the Senate as well. For Republicans, the task is to persuade their supporters that the contests remain open and to ensure that voters who have not participated early turn out on Tuesday.

The final results will show whether the patterns identified by the polls and forecasting models were temporary expressions of dissatisfaction or evidence of a broader change in American electoral politics.

Trump carried seven of the 11 battleground states in 2024, several by double-digit margins. Republicans believe that voters who supported him in those states could return to the polls and support Republican Senate candidates, even if the national political environment has shifted.

Fox also points to the number of undecided voters in Alaska, Iowa and Kansas. A late movement towards Republican candidates, combined with strong Election Day participation, could change the outcome.

The network’s analysis presents two possible scenarios: a Democratic gain that could give the party as many as 55 Senate seats, or a Republican performance strong enough to preserve a majority of up to 52. Either party needs to secure 51 seats in the Senate for a majority win.

The House picture is different. Fox’s final Power Rankings project that Democrats are likely to win at least 223 seats, with the possibility of reaching 240 in a strong performance. In the lower House of Representatives, the winner needs to gain at least 218 out of the 435 voting seats.

Other forecasts examine the changing political map.

The Wall Street Journal, reporting on the latest assessment by the Cook Political Report, said Democrats had become slight favourites to capture the Senate.

Cook identifies seven Senate races — Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Michigan, Ohio and Texas — as sufficiently competitive to remain within the margin of error.

For the House, Cook projects Democratic gains of between 12 and 25 seats, potentially giving the party a majority of as many as 240 members.

CBS News has also reported a sustained Democratic advantage in its House modelling. Its October 25 analysis, however, offered an important qualification: the Democratic lead had remained relatively stable rather than expanding, and voters who were still uncertain about participating tended to lean more Republican.

That distinction matters. A favourable polling environment does not necessarily mean that all voters expressing dissatisfaction with the administration will turn out on Election Day.

The Harvard model assigns probabilities to a possible Democratic takeover.

A forecast from the Harvard ElectIt project offers another way of assessing the congressional contests. The project provides three versions of its 2026 forecast: one based on its statistical election model, a second incorporating national generic-ballot polling and a third incorporating available state and district polls.

The underlying LogisTiCC model uses historical congressional election results and accounts for factors including incumbency, candidate-specific effects, strategic departures from office and the historical tendency of the president’s party to lose ground in midterm elections. The poll-based versions adjust the model using additional polling information.

Under the forecast configuration displayed in the Harvard link used for this report, Democrats have a 96pc probability of taking the House and a 79pc probability of gaining control of the Senate.

The model projects approximately 241 Democratic House seats, a net gain of 26, and 53 Democratic Senate seats, an increase of six.

The reported 95pc ranges are wide: 214 to 282 seats in the House and 47 to 57 in the Senate. These ranges underline that the figures are statistical estimates, not guaranteed outcomes.

The Senate projection is particularly significant because it illustrates how the model evaluates the possibility of Democrats overcoming the geographical disadvantages that have traditionally made the chamber difficult for them to capture.

The Harvard project cautions against treating a single projected seat count as a certain result. Its different forecast versions can produce different estimates as polling information changes.

Progressive politics and the changing Democratic coalition

The emerging political picture also reflects a longer evolution within the Democratic Party, particularly the growth of progressive politics and dissatisfaction with established political institutions.

Commentator Zeeshan Shah, a physician in Northern Virginia, believes Senator Bernie Sanders helped inject new energy into the progressive movement, creating political space for candidates challenging the Republican establishment.

After Sanders came New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who is believed to have taken that energy into the mainstream by directly challenging Trump and the politics associated with his administration, according to Mohsin Masood, a Virginia educationist.

Political science professor Farhat Haq believes Democrats could benefit from another pendulum swing in American politics, driven largely by dissatisfaction with Trump.

She points to rising living costs, the war involving Iran and the Gaza conflict as factors contributing to public discontent. Haq links the economic consequences of the Iran war to inflation and the pressure on household budgets.

She also argues that Trump has lost support among some of the groups that helped him politically, including Latino voters. Haq notes that PTI supporters in the United States, despite remaining politically active, are no longer supporting Trump as they did previously.

Together, these assessments suggest that the political shift may reflect more than the immediate circumstances of the campaign. Economic anxiety, foreign-policy disagreements and disappointment with established political leadership have all entered the debate over the direction of the country.

The final test comes on Tuesday

Republicans currently hold a 53-47 Senate majority, including two independents who caucus with Democrats. Democrats need a net gain of four seats to secure an outright 51-seat majority.

The House is a more straightforward target. Republicans hold a narrow majority, and the latest polling and election ratings point to a highly competitive contest for control.

A change in either chamber would significantly affect Trump’s ability to advance his legislative programme. Democratic control would also give the opposition party greater authority to investigate the administration and scrutinise its policies.

The final polls and forecasts show Democrats entering Election Day with opportunities in several states and congressional districts that were not widely expected to be competitive earlier in the campaign.

Yet polling error cannot be dismissed. Undecided voters, differences in turnout and the difficulty of predicting who will actually vote can all produce results that diverge from final surveys.

For Democrats, the election offers an opportunity to regain the House and potentially the Senate as well. For Republicans, the task is to persuade their supporters that the contests remain open and to ensure that voters who have not participated early turn out on Tuesday.

The final results will show whether the patterns identified by the polls and forecasting models were temporary expressions of dissatisfaction or evidence of a broader change in American electoral politics.

headline: China FM tells Iran official Beijing supports 'safeguarding sovereignty'
description: China’s top diplomat told a senior Iranian official that Beijing supports Tehran in “safeguarding its own...
article_text:
China’s top diplomat told a senior Iranian official that Beijing supports Tehran in “safeguarding its own sovereignty and security” as they met in the Chinese capital on Monday, after threats of renewed US strikes, AFP reports.

President Donald Trump said on Saturday that the United States has knocked out much of Iran’s military but still has to “take care of” one or two targets, as Tehran warned of reprisals if attacked.

“China supports Iran in safeguarding its own sovereignty and security,” Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi told Ali Bagheri Kani, the deputy secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, according to a statement from Beijing.

The foreign ministry had not previously announced the visit by Bagheri Kani to Beijing.

“All parties should… in a spirit of reason and pragmatism, focus on a political solution rather than once again resorting to armed conflict,” Wang told Bagheri Kani, according to the statement.

headline: Pakistan fined for slow over-rate in tri-series final
description: The hosts were found to be one over short after time allowances were taken into consideration by match referee Jeff Crowe of the Emirates ICC Elite Panel.
author: Dawn Sport
article_text:
Pakistan have been fined five per cent of their match fees for maintaining a slow over-rate during their three-wicket victory over Sri Lanka in the One-day International tri-series final in Lahore on Saturday.

The hosts were found to be one over short after time allowances were taken into consideration by match referee Jeff Crowe of the Emirates ICC Elite Panel, the International Cricket Council said in a statement on Monday.

Pakistan captain Shaheen Shah Afridi pleaded guilty to the offence and accepted the proposed sanction, which was imposed under Article 2.22 of the ICC Code of Conduct for Players and Player Support Personnel. The provision stipulates a fine of five per cent of a player’s match fee for every over his side fails to bowl within the allotted time.

The charge was levelled by on-field umpires Ahsan Raza and Wayne Knights, third umpire Sharfuddoula Ibne Shahid and fourth umpire Rashid Riaz.

Pakistan had conceded 325-8 in the final before chasing down the target of 326 with three wickets and nine balls to spare, securing the tri-series title in front of their home crowd at Gaddafi Stadium.

Fakhar Zaman led the successful chase with 127 off 99 balls, hitting 11 fours and six sixes to register his 12th ODI century. His innings helped Pakistan recover from an early collapse and complete a joint-record successful chase in an ODI final.

headline: Consumer inflation falls to 9.6pc in Oct from 10.3pc in Sept
description: According to the statistics bureau, decrease recorded mainly due to a slight slowdown in perishable food products.
author: Mubarak Zeb Khan
article_text:
ISLAMABAD: Consumer inflation eased to 9.6 per cent in October from 10.3pc a month earlier, mainly due to a slight slowdown in perishable food products, the Pakistan Bureau of Statistics said on Monday.

The slowdown in the inflation rate for the second consecutive month, measured by the Consumer Price Index, reversed the sharp increase recorded in August, when higher food and energy prices pushed the annual rate to 11.1pc from 9.2pc in July.

The easing was recorded in both places, in rural areas where inflation fell to 9.5pc from 10.1pc, while urban inflation edged down to 9.8pc from 10.5pc.

The October reading was also within the Ministry of Finance’s projection of 9.5pc to 10.5pc for the month in its Monthly Economic Update and Outlook for October. According to the finance ministry, easing headline inflation offers some relief, while improved crop supplies can help ease food price pressures.

However, despite the decline in the annual rate, prices rose 1.1pc month-on-month in October. The annual inflation rate was 6.2pc in October last year.

The average inflation between July and October stood at 10.05pc compared with 4.79pc over the corresponding period last year.

The easing was largely driven by perishable food prices. Food inflation dropped to 7.8pc in urban areas in October from 8.1pc in September. The decline was much sharper in rural areas, where food inflation fell to 7.1pc from 7.7pc a month earlier.

However, non-food inflation moved in the opposite direction, indicating continued pressure on household expenses. Urban non-food inflation decelerated to 10.6pc from 11.5pc in September, while rural non-food inflation fell to 12.3pc from 13.1pc.

The latest data shows that the composition of inflation shifted in October. While food inflation slowed sharply, electricity and transport costs continued to rise. Electricity charges increased by 8.50pc from the previous month, while transport prices rose by 30.39pc in urban areas.

At the national level, transport costs increased by 1.79pc during October from the previous month and were 28.61pc higher than in the same month last year. Housing, water, electricity, gas and fuels increased by 0.25pc during the month and by 11.03pc on an annual basis.

Core inflation, which excludes volatile food and energy components, also eased slightly. It stood at 7.8pc in urban areas in October, compared with 8.6pc in September, while the rural rate declined to 7.1pc from 8.1pc.

ISLAMABAD: Consumer inflation eased to 9.6 per cent in October from 10.3pc a month earlier, mainly due to a slight slowdown in perishable food products, the Pakistan Bureau of Statistics said on Monday.

The slowdown in the inflation rate for the second consecutive month, measured by the Consumer Price Index, reversed the sharp increase recorded in August, when higher food and energy prices pushed the annual rate to 11.1pc from 9.2pc in July.

The easing was recorded in both places, in rural areas where inflation fell to 9.5pc from 10.1pc, while urban inflation edged down to 9.8pc from 10.5pc.

The October reading was also within the Ministry of Finance’s projection of 9.5pc to 10.5pc for the month in its Monthly Economic Update and Outlook for October. According to the finance ministry, easing headline inflation offers some relief, while improved crop supplies can help ease food price pressures.

However, despite the decline in the annual rate, prices rose 1.1pc month-on-month in October. The annual inflation rate was 6.2pc in October last year.

The average inflation between July and October stood at 10.05pc compared with 4.79pc over the corresponding period last year.

The easing was largely driven by perishable food prices. Food inflation dropped to 7.8pc in urban areas in October from 8.1pc in September. The decline was much sharper in rural areas, where food inflation fell to 7.1pc from 7.7pc a month earlier.

However, non-food inflation moved in the opposite direction, indicating continued pressure on household expenses. Urban non-food inflation decelerated to 10.6pc from 11.5pc in September, while rural non-food inflation fell to 12.3pc from 13.1pc.

The latest data shows that the composition of inflation shifted in October. While food inflation slowed sharply, electricity and transport costs continued to rise. Electricity charges increased by 8.50pc from the previous month, while transport prices rose by 30.39pc in urban areas.

At the national level, transport costs increased by 1.79pc during October from the previous month and were 28.61pc higher than in the same month last year. Housing, water, electricity, gas and fuels increased by 0.25pc during the month and by 11.03pc on an annual basis.

Core inflation, which excludes volatile food and energy components, also eased slightly. It stood at 7.8pc in urban areas in October, compared with 8.6pc in September, while the rural rate declined to 7.1pc from 8.1pc.

article_text:
Former US president Bill Clinton has criticised the US attack on Iran, saying the rise in petrol prices is a direct consequence of a military operation that was not carefully planned.

He said wars should not be started without a clear plan to end the fighting and prevent further loss of life.

Clinton also criticised what he described as corruption and vanity projects in the Trump administration.

headline: Araghchi, Meredov discuss regional developments, economic cooperation
description: Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has held talks with his Turkmen counterpart Rashid Meredov in Ashgabat,...
article_text:
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has held talks with his Turkmen counterpart Rashid Meredov in Ashgabat, focusing on strengthening bilateral cooperation and reviewing regional and international developments, IRNA reports.

Araghchi met with Meredov, who also serves as Deputy Chairman of the Cabinet of Ministers of Turkmenistan, on Monday, during a one-day visit to the Central Asian country.

The two officials reviewed the latest developments in Tehran-Ashgabat relations and emphasised the need to capitalise on existing capacities to expand cooperation across various political and economic fields.

Meredov highlighted the historical ties between the two neighbouring countries, describing them as a solid foundation for further strengthening bilateral relations.

headline: Forget my phone, can hackers access my fridge?
description: If a device is connected to the internet, directly or through an app, cloud service or home network, it can potentially be hacked.
author: Reuters
article_text:
Ahold Delhaize said on Monday that an “IT incident” had hit fridges and freezers in dozens of its supermarkets in Belgium and Luxembourg.

In October, the retailer reported an earlier cybersecurity incident to the Dutch police, coinciding with a cyberattack in France that caused refrigerators and freezers at hundreds of stores to heat up to 50°Celsius overnight, sparking fires and spoiling food.

From refrigerators and heating systems to security cameras and alarm networks, an expanding range of devices once largely mechanical can now be monitored and controlled remotely, creating new opportunities for cybercriminals.

Can hackers really get into my fridge?

In theory, yes. If a device is connected to the internet, directly or through an app, cloud service or home network, it can potentially be hacked.

In 2015, researchers demonstrated at a Las Vegas hacking conference how a Samsung smart refrigerator could be compromised, allowing them to intercept some of the internet traffic passing through the device.

In many cases, attackers are more interested in stealing data, disrupting services or using connected devices as a way into a larger network.

What household devices could be hacked?

The most common targets are devices connected to the internet and controlled remotely. These include security cameras, video doorbells, alarm systems, smart locks, thermostats and central heating systems.

Smart appliances such as refrigerators, ovens and washing machines can also be vulnerable if they are connected to the wider internet. Even some toothbrushes are now internet-connected.

Routers, not appliances, account for more than three-quarters of all attacks on connected devices, according to security-industry data.

The number of such devices has grown rapidly as manufacturers have added internet connectivity to products that were once entirely mechanical.

What could a hacker actually do?

Once inside a device, a hacker can generally do one of two things: gather information or take control of the device.

A camera can show the inside of a home, a device with a microphone can pick up sound, and a compromised router can expose everything that travels through the network.

Hackers who take control of a device can switch it on or off, change settings or lock users out of their accounts. A compromised thermostat could affect heating, while a hacked freezer or refrigerator could disrupt temperature controls.

In more serious cases, attackers may use poorly secured devices to gain access to other systems on the same network or to steal personal information linked to online accounts.

Could hackers take over my car, electricity or water supply?

Cybersecurity researchers have repeatedly demonstrated vulnerabilities in connected vehicles.

In 2015, researchers remotely took control of a moving Jeep through its internet-connected entertainment system, forcing the recall of about 1.4 million vehicles and the deployment of software fixes.

Nearly a decade later, researchers disclosed a flaw that allowed them to track, unlock and start certain Kia vehicles using only a licence plate number. The researchers said they reported the vulnerabilities to Kia, which fixed them within months, and there was no evidence they had been exploited in real-world attacks.

Modern vehicles and aircraft are also designed with extensive safety and backup systems.

Critical infrastructure such as power and water networks generally has multiple layers of security, monitoring and regulation that are not present in consumer devices.

That does not mean they are immune from cyberattacks, but they are typically much harder targets than a household appliance connected to a home Wi-Fi network.

How can people protect their devices?

Cybersecurity experts generally recommend changing default passwords, enabling two-factor authentication where available, and regularly installing software updates.

Consumers should also remove or replace devices that no longer receive security updates, keep most devices on a local network and only connect products to the wider internet when there is a clear reason to do so.

The simplest rule is often the most effective: the fewer connected devices you have, the fewer potential entry points exist for attackers.

Cybersecurity experts generally recommend changing default passwords, enabling two-factor authentication where available, and regularly installing software updates.

Consumers should also remove or replace devices that no longer receive security updates, keep most devices on a local network and only connect products to the wider internet when there is a clear reason to do so.

headline: TotalEnergies chief sees no gas shortage in Europe this winter
description: Europe will not face a gas shortage this winter; it will simply be forced to pay more to ensure sufficient supply,...
article_text:
Europe will not face a gas shortage this winter; it will simply be forced to pay more to ensure sufficient supply, Reuters reports quoting TotalEnergies Chief Executive Officer Patrick Pouyanne.

“The idea of a gas shortage is wrong,” Pouyanne tells a briefing on the company’s energy demand outlook, adding that Europe is only waking up to its gas storage needs after markets had bet on the Iran war ending in the summer.

headline: Civilian convicted of offences against state cannot claim fundamental rights, govt says in report to LHC
description: Report argues that Imran's nephew Hassaan Niazi is a convicted prisoner and that his release through a second round of litigation, other than by way of appeal, is not permissible.
author: Wajih Ahmad Sheikh
article_text:
LAHORE: The Punjab government on Monday informed the Lahore High Court (LHC) that a civilian who commits an offence against the state and is convicted cannot claim the protection of fundamental rights.

The response came as the government sought the dismissal of a petition filed by Barrister Hassaan Khan Niazi, nephew of PTI founder Imran Khan, challenging his handover to the army and subsequent trial in a case related to the May 9 riots.

In a report submitted after almost a year on behalf of the provincial government through the home secretary and the inspector general of police, the deputy inspector general of police (legal) said every citizen’s first duty was loyalty to the state, citing a 2005 LHC judgment (PLD 2005 LAH 721).

The report described Niazi as a convicted prisoner, arguing that his release through a second round of litigation, other than by way of appeal, was not permissible.

It said no judicial order was required for his handover because Niazi was neither in judicial custody nor on remand.

The report further stated that he was an absconder, unlike the 16 co-accused whose transfer had been sought from an anti-terrorism court while they were in jail.

The Sarwar Road station house officer neither handed over Niazi’s custody nor received a letter from the commanding officer, the report added.

“That was done by the investigation in-charge of the Sarwar Road police station, who is not a party to the petition,” the report claimed.

It stated that the Supreme Court’s May 7, 2025, ruling on the intra-court appeals upheld military trials while granting the accused the right to appeal, but not the right to file constitutional petitions.

It said Niazi had already filed an appeal under Section 133-B of the Pakistan Army Act, 1952.

“It is a well-established principle that the same question of law cannot be challenged in two different forums simultaneously; therefore, this petition lacks maintainability in the eyes of the law,” the report maintained.

It further argued that Niazi had misread the Supreme Court’s short order, which applied only to petitions pending or filed against anti-terrorism court orders.

It accused him of concealing facts about his appeal, his father Hafeezullah Khan Niazi’s earlier proceedings, including a petition before the apex court and a contempt petition, as well as the anti-terrorism court’s May 25, 2023, order.

The report said Niazi had not annexed the military court’s order, an objection upheld by the high court in two other petitions.

It prayed the court to dismiss the petition on the grounds that it was devoid of merit and not maintainable.

According to the report, Niazi was a proclaimed offender in FIR No. 96/2023, registered on May 10, 2023, at the Sarwar Road police station in Lahore Cantonment in connection with an attack on Jinnah House, which was also the residence of the Lahore Corps commander.

Police arrested Niazi in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa on Aug 16, 2023. The next day, the commanding officer of the 54 Electrical and Mechanical Engineers Battalion, Lahore, asked for his custody, saying his alleged offences fell under the Official Secrets Act, 1923 and the Pakistan Army Act, 1952 and were triable by court-martial.

Police handed him over under Section 76 of the Army Act, read with Section 549(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure. He was later sentenced to ten years’ imprisonment in December 2024.

Defence ministry’s reply

The defence ministry told the LHC that Niazi went to Jinnah House on May 9, 2023, where he made videos and passed sarcastic remarks about the Corps Commander’s uniform.

“The incident impacted the image of Pakistan and was prejudicial to the safety and interest of the state,” said a reply signed by an assistant judge advocate general, the army’s legal branch at Headquarters 4 Corps, and filed through an additional attorney general.

The reply said that Niazi, held at Kot Lakhpat Jail, was convicted by a Field General Court Martial (FGCM) and sentenced to 10 years’ rigorous imprisonment under Section 3 of the Official Secrets Act, 1923, read with Section 59 of the Army Act.

It argued that the petition was barred by Articles 199(3) and 8(3) of the Constitution, xcludes matters related to the proceedings of the armed forces personnel from the purview of the high courts, and that Niazi already had an appeal pending under Section 133-B of the Army Act before the army court of appeals.

It said the SC’s May 7, 2025 short order restored Sections 2(1)(d) and 59(4) of the Army Act without striking down Section 133-B.

The direction that high courts decide petitions “on their own merits”, the reply said, is not a blanket exemption from the constitutional bar. It said Niazi was tried with a counsel of his choice and made a judicial confession before a magistrate that he did not retract at trial.

It said the trial ended on Jan 5, 2024 and he was admitted to Lahore’s Central Jail on Dec 26, 2024. It also argued that he had waited nearly two years before coming to court.

The defence ministry’s reply pointed out that Niazi was taken into military custody under Section 549(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure.

It denied discrimination under Article 25, saying that protesters involved in ordinary disruption were tried by the antiterrorism courts, whereas Niazi’s alleged offence involved a prohibited military installation.

A joint trial with the ordinary accused was legally impossible, it said, adding that no Official Secrets Act case had gone to an ordinary court so far.

It added that weekly phone calls and meetings with Niazi’s family were arranged after the handover.

The ministry asked the court to dismiss the petition as premature, not maintainable and without merit, pleading that the Constitution barred the high court from hearing cases involving persons subject to the Pakistan Army Act, 1952.
